How Bravo escaped enemy territory alive after Iranian forces downed jet
item.description:
“I’m hurt, I’m moving, God is good.”
That’s the first message the Pentagon received from US weapons systems officer Dude 44 Bravo after Iranian forces downed his jet, leaving him stranded in its heartland.
What follows is an audacious rescue attempt, told by the US serviceman and officials for the first time.
In April, Iran shot down an F-15E jet, catapulting two US crew members “deep inside enemy territory”.
While the pilot was rescued in a matter of hours, the jet’s weapons systems officer, known as Dude 44 Bravo, was missing in Iran for nearly two days, scaling mountain ridges while “seriously wounded”.
In an interview with US’s 60 Minutes program, he detailed his experience evading Iranian bounty hunters and surviving the rugged terrain without food or water.
Bravo, who was only referred to by his codename, said the day began like any other until his F-15E jet, which costs about $30million, was shot down by a shoulder-fired Iranian missile.
When Bravo and the jet’s pilot, codenamed Alpha, were unable to save the plane, they decided to both eject.
As Bravo was “floating over the heart of Iran”, he realised his parachute was damaged.
“That was the most terrifying thing I’d ever seen,” he told reporter Nora O’Donnell, saying he had prayed to God to help him through.
Bravo estimated he hit the ground at a speed of 70-100mph.
The impact left him with a broken back, arm and shoulder but somehow alive.
“[It was] a modern-day miracle,” Bravo said.
“I believe it’s a testament to God’s provision in my life to bring me through that moment in a way that didn’t prevent injuries but prevented any catastrophic injuries that would have affected my ability to survive.”
His pilot Alpha, meanwhile, was nowhere to be seen.
The pair had fallen about 8 kilometres apart in the rugged Iranian terrain.
Badly injured and stranded in a valley surrounded by cliffs, Bravo mustered the strength to climb a 7,000-foot ridge line to avoid being captured by Iranians.
On state television, Iranian authorities had already issued a bounty for both service members.
“Never let a lack of motivation put you on Iranian TV,” Bravo said of his determination to scale the mountain.
The 60 Minutes interview has been viewed by the Pentagon as a major opportunity “to craft the narrative around the Iran war which has becoming increasingly unpopular”, according to CNN.
In particular, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had been “unusually hands-on”.
The Defense Secretary was featured in the program, describing the moment he discovered the jet had been downed behind enemy lines.
“Probably s***,” he said, when asked of his initial reaction.
“You always knew that was possible, so immediately it’s to the next steps: ‘Are they OK? Does Iran know that?’”
US bombers launched strikes on nearby Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps members in a mission that included an additional 92 personnel.
Those 92 represented the first US boots on Iranian ground in 46 years, Admiral Brad Cooper said.
“It was a gunfight, all the way in and all the way out,” Hegseth said.
The downed jet was later blown up by US forces to prevent it from falling into Iranian hands.
After making first contact, Bravo was located with the help of CIA technology.
Bird helicopters then helped reach Bravo on the ridge line after more than 50 hours inside Iran.
He was rescued by elite para-rescue service members known as PJs.
“The moment a PJ showed up to me on that ridge line was one of the greatest moments of my life,” Bravo said.
While he said he would not share their first words to him, his were simple: “Let’s go.”
The PJs moved him toward a secret rendezvous point before dawn.
But as they did, the two C-130 transport aircraft that had ferried in the 92 personnel suffered a mechanical failure and could not take off from the makeshift airstrip.
Their commanders made a high-risk decision, ordering additional aircraft to fly into Iran to extract the group in waves.
“We had more than 90 of America’s most elite service members on the ground, and our focus at that point was to make sure we got them safely out,” Admiral Cooper said.
General Dan Caine said on the program that Bravo’s jet had been conducting strikes on Iran’s drone and missile facilities.
He said the number of personnel deployed for the rescue was worth it.
“We would have sent more to go get the back seater.”
As he thanked those who rescued him, Bravo said:
“This is not a story about what I went through.
“It’s a story of the teamwork, the training, of the faith, or the decisions, of the leadership.
“To do something that will live in history as a example of what America’s willing to do in order to uphold our promise and leave no man behind.”

item.title: From Delhi to Makkah: Bangladesh’s calculated political gamble?
item.description:
The uncertainty surrounding Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to India and Dhaka’s growing interest in the Makkah Defense Pact are being viewed as possible signs of a shift in Bangladesh’s foreign-policy calculations. But for Tarique Rahman, this is unlikely to be a sudden or whimsical decision. Politically, it appears to be a carefully calculated move.
The proposed India visit has yet to take place, despite an invitation from New Delhi and discussions over possible dates. But the timing has become complicated.
The uncertainty reflects how difficult India-Bangladesh relations have become since Sheikh Hasina was ousted in August 2024 and fled to India.
Her continued stay in India has become one of the biggest contentious issues between the two neighbours. Bangladesh has repeatedly sought her extradition after a tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia in November 2025 over her role in the deadly crackdown on the 2024 student-led uprising. Hasina has rejected the proceedings as politically motivated.
Against this backdrop, anti-India sentiment grew in Bangladesh after the fall of the Awami League government. “Delhi or Dhaka? Dhaka, Dhaka” became a popular political slogan, reflecting a growing perception among sections of the public that Bangladesh should reduce its dependence on India.
But the BNP government cannot simply turn away from New Delhi.
India is Bangladesh’s most important geographical neighbour, sharing a more than 4,000-kilometre border and deep economic, security, and cultural ties. Whatever political differences exist between the two governments, geography makes a working relationship unavoidable.
That makes Rahman’s decision over an India visit particularly sensitive.
On August 5, Hasina, speaking from India in her first media interaction since her ouster, said she intended to return to Bangladesh in December. She said she was prepared to face detention or even death.
Among the questions from journalists was whether she would visit the shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi before returning to Bangladesh. Hasina responded positively.
Visiting religious shrines, particularly Islamic shrines, is not new for Bangladeshi politicians. Before national election campaigns, leaders from major political parties often visit shrines, both as a cultural tradition and as a way of connecting with voters.
Around 90% of Bangladesh’s population is Muslim, and political parties have long sought to tap into religious sentiment when building support for major political moves.
Meanwhile, Hasina’s remarks triggered a sharp reaction from Dhaka, which criticized India for allowing her to address the media from its territory.
For Rahman, visiting India while Hasina remains there therefore carries an obvious political risk.
His government emerged from the political forces that opposed Hasina and her Awami League. A visit to New Delhi at this moment could raise questions among those forces about whether Dhaka was making concessions over Hasina or seeking a political accommodation with India.
It could create mistrust, or even divisions, among the pro-July forces.
Rahman therefore appears to have little political incentive to take that risk at this stage. Instead, he appears intent on keeping the pro-July forces together, despite their differences, as they seek to politically counter the Awami League in the coming days, much as they did in 2024.
And then came another event.
Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman invited Rahman to visit Saudi Arabia. Saudi Ambassador Abdullah Zafer H bin Abiyah delivered the invitation on August 17.
The invitation came at a time when Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan had signed the much-discussed Makkah Joint Defense Agreement.
Signed in Makkah on August 7, the agreement states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all three, making it similar in principle to NATO’s collective-defense clause.
The defense pact could also expand beyond its three founding members. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Egypt is the most likely next member, noting that the four countries already cooperate like alliance partners. Turkey has also said the pact is not directed against any country, including Iran, and does not replace existing alliances.
The Makkah Agreement has inevitably drawn comparisons with the Cold War-era Central Treaty Organization, or CENTO, which included Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, Iraq, and Britain. Although the United States supported CENTO through bilateral defense agreements, it never became a member. The alliance ultimately failed to develop an effective collective defense mechanism and dissolved in 1979 following Iran’s revolution.
That history raises questions about whether the Makkah Agreement could face similar challenges.
For Bangladesh, however, the more immediate question is why it would want to join such a pact.
Dhaka has expressed interest in joining, but it has not received an invitation.
“If they express an intention to include Bangladesh in the pact, we will certainly consider it positively,” Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament on August 27. He also made clear that Bangladesh’s inclusion was not currently under discussion.
That distinction is important. Bangladesh is not joining the Makkah Pact. It is signaling that it would consider joining if invited.
Yet even that signal is politically significant.
The pact brings together three countries with very different strategic interests but substantial military and political weight. For Bangladesh, closer engagement with them could open another channel of diplomacy beyond its traditional relationships with India, China, the United States, and Japan.
But it could also complicate those relationships.
For a developing Asian country like Bangladesh, the central question is simple: What security problem would joining the Makkah Pact actually solve?
Bangladesh does not face the same immediate security environment as Saudi Arabia, Turkey, or Pakistan. It is not in the Middle East and does not face the regional military threats that shaped the pact.
Its security concerns are primarily regional, including its relationship with India, border management, maritime security, and the wider stability of the Bay of Bengal.
Joining a defense pact centered on countries thousands of kilometres away would therefore require a clear strategic justification.
There could be benefits.
Bangladesh is a Muslim-majority country of more than 170 million people and has deep economic and social links with the Gulf.
Millions of Bangladeshis work in the Middle East, making Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states important sources of remittances.
Closer relations could therefore bring economic as well as diplomatic benefits.
The pact could also give Dhaka another platform through which to engage with influential Muslim-majority countries.
But the risks may be greater than the immediate security benefits.
India is likely to watch Bangladesh’s interests in possible participation closely. New Delhi has a longstanding strategic rivalry with Pakistan, while India and Bangladesh share a border of more than 4,000 kilometres.
The growing military ties between Dhaka and Islamabad in the last two years have also raised concerns in New Delhi. India has previously accused Bangladesh of allowing northeastern Indian insurgents to operate from its territory, allegedly with Pakistani support. Bangladesh and Pakistan denied those allegations.
For Dhaka, the challenge is therefore to deepen ties with Pakistan and the wider Muslim world without allowing India to see the move as a strategic alignment against it.
India is Bangladesh’s neighbour and cannot be replaced by a distant strategic partner. Saudi Arabia is an important economic and religious partner, but it cannot offer Bangladesh what India does simply because of geography.
Pakistan, meanwhile, carries its own complicated history with Bangladesh.
The Makkah Pact could nevertheless give Rahman additional diplomatic space if he uses it as part of a broader strategy of diversification. But if it becomes a perceived anti-India or pro-Pakistan alignment, it could create exactly the kind of regional tensions Bangladesh has traditionally sought to avoid.
This is where the political gamble lies.
For Rahman, the Makkah Pact could also prove to be a politically useful card at home, particularly for mobilizing support among anti-India groups and Bangladesh’s Muslim majority ahead of Hasina’s planned return.
And in Bangladesh, this kind of political symbolism is not unusual.
Even former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina was given the title “Qawmi Janani,” or “Mother of Qawmi,” ahead of the 2018 general elections after her government formally recognized Qawmi madrasa degrees.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman also met Hefazat Ameer Shah Muhibullah Babunagari in Chittagong on August 9, asking the religious pressure group to continue its support for the BNP.
With this signal on the Makkah Pact, it would not be surprising if a new slogan emerged on the streets of Dhaka: “Delhi or Makkah? Makkah, Makkah.” Whether such a slogan actually emerges remains to be seen, but the political narrative is already taking shape.
The move could help bring the pro-July forces together to counter the Awami League as Hasina’s expected return in December approaches.
In fact, BNP’s calculated view toward Makkah, and its attempt to connect Bangladesh’s foreign policy with the symbolism of Islam’s holiest city, could do more than solidify the position among Islamist groups, even the parliamentary opposition party Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, which has welcomed the idea of Bangladesh considering participation in the pact.
And that could certainly become a political test of Sheikh Hasina’s determination to return to Dhaka.
In Bangladesh’s complex political landscape, where religion and politics remain deeply intertwined, this diplomatic dance carries consequences far beyond international relations.
For Tarique Rahman, it is a gamble over both foreign policy and domestic political supremacy.
Sardar Ronie is a Bangladesh-based journalist with nearly 16 years of experience covering politics, human rights, and regional issues for international outlets including BBC News, DW Asia, and Al Arabiya English, bringing stories from the ground to global audiences. He can be reached at sardarronie@gmail.com .

item.title: Community Bank celebrates 7th anniversary
item.description:
Community Bank Bangladesh PLC. celebrated its 7th anniversary with a commitment to moving towards new heights through transformation, growth and sustainability, following seven years of achievements and experiences.
The day was marked by various programs organized by the bank’s officials and employees. Building on its achievements over the past seven years and harnessing future opportunities, they expressed their determination to advance the bank as a more modern, technology-driven and sustainable banking institution.
As part of the anniversary celebration, Inspector General of Police, Bangladesh and chairman of Community Bank Bangladesh PLC Md Ali Hossain Fakir cut the anniversary cake at Police Headquarters.
Also present at the event were Md Akram Hossain, Additional IGP (Finance), Bangladesh Police; Kazi Md Fazlul Karim, Additional IG and Rector, Police Staff College, Bangladesh Police; Md Kamrul Ahsan, Deputy Inspector General (Confidential), Bangladesh Police; Ahmad Muyeed, Additional DIG, Bangladesh Police Kallyan Trust, Bangladesh Police; Kamrul Hasan Talukdar, Inspector, Bangladesh Police; Md Morshed Hasan Khan, independent director; Syed Rafiqul Haq, independent director; Mohammed Tofazzul Hussain, independent director; Mohammed Emtiaz Uddin, managing director, Community Bank Bangladesh PLC . ; along with senior officials of the bank.
At the event, Chairman of Community Bank Bangladesh PLC and Inspector General of Police, Bangladesh Md Ali Hossain Fakir said: “The trust and capabilities that Community Bank has built over the past seven years are a matter of great pride. We look forward to the bank playing an even more important role in the country’s economic progress by ensuring more modern, customer-friendly and sustainable banking services in the future.”
Managing Director Mohammed Emtiaz Uddin said: “Our commitment on the occasion of Community Bank’s 7th anniversary is to make the bank stronger and take it to new heights through transformation, growth and sustainability in the days ahead.”
He added: “In its seven years of operation, Community Bank has built a strong foundation. This achievement is an inspiration for our future journey. Alongside further improving technology, innovation and service quality in line with the changing banking sector, we must give the highest priority to our customers’ trust and expectations. At the same time, we must further strengthen our contribution to the country’s economic progress through responsible and sustainable banking.”
The Head Office of Community Bank also wore a festive look on the occasion.
Managing Director Mohammed Emtiaz Uddin, along with officials and employees from different levels of the bank, cut the anniversary cake to celebrate the 7th anniversary.
The occasion created an atmosphere of joy and emotion among the officials and employees as they reflected on the memories, achievements and experiences of the bank’s seven-year journey.
Following the celebration, the bank’s officials and employees shared memories, experiences and achievements from its seven-year journey. Their reflections brought forward the story of an institution’s growth, the experience of overcoming various challenges and the many memorable moments of their professional association with Community Bank.
Building on the achievements of the past seven years and embracing the promise of a new beginning, the officials and employees renewed their commitment to moving forward with greater determination, dedication and confidence.
They expressed their aspiration that, through collective efforts, technology-driven innovation, continuous improvement and sustainable growth, Community Bank will play an even more important and responsible role in the financial progress of Bangladesh in the years ahead.
At the same time, Community Bank aims to establish itself as a trusted, sustainable and cashless Bank in Bangladesh by 2029.

item.title: ShareTrip joins Monitor Airline of the Year 2026 as title sponsor
item.description:
ShareTrip has joined the 12 th edition of Monitor Airline of the Year as the title sponsor.
The annual awards, organized by The Bangladesh Monitor, is the country’s only airline recognition program.
The title sponsorship was formalized through the signing of a MoU by Kazi Wahidul Alam, editor of The Bangladesh Monitor, and Sadia Haque, co-founder and CEO of ShareTrip Limited, at a ceremony held at Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport on September 10.
Under the MoU, ShareTrip will extend its support to The Bangladesh Monitor in promoting the award program and organizing the gala award ceremony.
The ShareTrip-Monitor Airline of the Year 2026 awards will recognize airlines operating in Bangladesh for excellence in passenger service across 27 categories.
The winners will be determined primarily on the basis of an opinion poll among frequent air travelers.
The online voting was conducted from July 21 to August 25, 2026.
Individuals who undertook at least four air trips during 2025 were eligible to participate in the poll and cast their votes based on their personal travel experiences.
A high-profile jury comprising representatives from diverse social and professional groups will select the winners based on the results of the opinion poll.
The winners will be formally announced at a gala award ceremony scheduled to be held at Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport in November.
Airline of the Year is the flagship event of The Bangladesh Monitor.
The program was introduced in 2007 and has since been organized regularly to recognize airlines for their service excellence.

item.title: Customer harassment alleged over irregularities at Kashiani Palli Bidyut Samity
item.description:
Customers of the Kashiani Palli Bidyut Samity in Gopalganj have alleged harassment over frequent load-shedding, unusually high electricity bills, discrepancies in meter readings and the collection of money for services, among other alleged irregularities.
Frequent power outages, coupled with alleged arbitrary practices by officials and employees, have sparked growing dissatisfaction among customers in the area.
Customers said electricity goes out several times a day and sometimes remains unavailable for hours, disrupting daily life as well as electricity-dependent businesses.
Ariful Islam Abhi, a businessman at Kashiani Sadar Bazar, said his establishment has three refrigerators, two fans and five lights. His monthly electricity bill normally ranges between Tk3,500 and Tk5,000.
However, he said a combined bill of Tk38,147 was issued for May, June and July.
Abhi said he visited the Kashiani Rural Electricity Office seeking an explanation and a solution but did not receive any relief. Instead, he was allegedly pressured to pay the unusually high bill.
He said the financial burden and repeated harassment eventually forced him to shut down his business.
Another customer, Shariful Islam of Hiranyakandi village, alleged that his meter showed 70 units of consumption in April, while he was billed for 140 units in May.
He said the meter reading showed "zero" in June, July and August, but he was nevertheless billed for 140 units in each of those months.
After failing to resolve the issue at the electricity office, Shariful Islam filed an online complaint with the Directorate of National Consumers’ Right Protection.
He said officials later went to his house to remove the meter, but he prevented them from doing so. Following an investigation, his electricity bills were adjusted.
Meanwhile, allegations have also been raised over the installation of an additional electricity pole and provision of a connection at the home of a customer, Israfil Molla, in Orakandi village.
According to information gathered during an inquiry, the nearest service pole was about 130 feet from Molla’s house. As an additional pole was reportedly required due to objections from a neighbour, he contacted the Ramdia Sub-Zonal Office.
The office subsequently issued a demand note of Tk28,148 for construction of a one-span line.
However, it has been alleged that after collecting a substantial amount of money from the customer, officials of the Kashiani office installed the pole and provided the connection without informing the Ramdia office.
No record of the Tk28,148 being deposited with the Ramdia office was found, according to the allegations.
Customers have raised several similar complaints against the Kashiani Rural Electricity Office, including allegations of unofficial payments for services.
Golam Faruk Mir, deputy general manager of the Kashiani Zonal Office of Palli Bidyut Samity said the allegations would be investigated.
Regarding the alleged non-deposit of the demand-note money, he said the customer had received the connection free of charge and in accordance with the rules.

item.title: Hill Women’s Federation adopts seven-point proposals
item.description:
The Hill Women’s Federation has adopted a seven-point political proposal, including formal government talks with the United People’s Democratic Front (UPDF).
The proposals were adopted unanimously at a special women’s conference of the federation held in Dighinala, Khagrachhari, on Sunday, said a press release.
The organization demanded the immediate withdrawal of all cases, including what it described as politically motivated and fabricated cases, filed during the previous regime, as well as the unconditional release of all political prisoners, including UPDF leader Ananda Prakash Chakma, and members of the Bawm community detained in Bandarban.
It also called for legal action against armed groups allegedly involved in various crimes and demanded an end to arbitrary arrests, harassment and raids by security forces.
The federation demanded that hill people be guaranteed their constitutional right, as citizens of Bangladesh, to hold peaceful meetings and rallies in the CHT.
It also called for the implementation in the CHT of legal measures taken in Dhaka against those accused of rape and murder of women and children, saying this was necessary to ensure their safety.
The organization further demanded the arrest and exemplary punishment of Lt Ferdous and others identified as suspects in the abduction of Kalpana Chakma, saying such action would help restore public confidence in the rule of law in the hills.
It demanded the publication of investigation reports and exemplary punishment for those responsible for the killings, destruction and looting during the September 19-20, 2024 incidents in Dighinala, Khagrachhari and Rangamati, and the September 28, 2025 incident in Guimara. It also called for investigations into killings that have occurred in the hills at different times.
The final proposal called for an immediate halt to hill cutting and the construction of border roads, as well as a ban on planting foreign tree species, to protect forests, nature, the environment and biodiversity.
Around 60 representatives and observers from different branches of the organisation took part in the conference and endorsed the proposals by a show of hands. The proposals were subsequently adopted unanimously.
At the first session, Hill Women’s Federation President Niti Chakma presided, while General Secretary Rita Chakma conducted the session. Parbatya Nari Sangha President Kanika Dewan, UPDF organizer Mantu Chakma, Pahari Chhatra Parishad President Samir Chakma, and Ganatantrik Jubo Forum Central Member Anupam Chakma took seats on the stage.
Hill Women’s Federation Central Member Jesi Chakma delivered the welcome address.

item.title: Police AC, 2 ASIs withdrawn over businessman abduction, Tk 1.8m embezzlement
item.description:
A police assistant commissioner (AC) and two assistant sub-inspectors (ASIs) have been withdrawn from duty following allegations that they abducted a businessman and his friend in Chattogram city and embezzled Tk 1.8 million from them.

Chattogram Metropolitan Police Commissioner Hasan Md Shawkat Ali ordered their withdrawal from duty on Monday.

The withdrawn officers are AC Shariful Alam Chowdhury of the city police’s LIC branch, ASI Bashir Uddin and ASI Md Sufian of the Ration Branch.

The authorities have attached AC Shariful to the city police headquarters, while the two ASIs have been attached to Dampara police lines.

CMP Commissioner Hasan Md Shawkat Ali told Prothom Alo on Monday that they had formed an investigation committee, headed by Deputy Commissioner (PMO) Md Badruzzaman, to investigate the incident.

According to police and people concerned, DB police, identifying themselves as such, picked up businessman Akhtaruzzaman Shakil and his friend Md Mansur from the K-Block area of Halishahar police station on 4 September.

Police had information that Shakil was an agent for online gambling and that his mobile phone contained a substantial amount of cryptocurrency, or Binance dollars.

The allegations state that officers took them to the LIC branch on the ground floor of the CMP office. There, AC Shariful allegedly initially demanded Tk 10 million (1 crore) from them in his office.

Following negotiations, the matter was allegedly settled with 12,500 Binance dollars held on Shakil’s mobile phone and Tk 1 million (10 lakh) in cash.

Shakil alleged that officers initially transferred US$10,500 from his Binance account to another account in three transactions. Later, they converted Tk 600,000 from City Bank into dollars through Binance and took the money.

They also took him to a BRAC Bank ATM booth near Dampara police lines and made him withdraw more money. They allegedly collected another Tk 80,000 through a mobile financial service app.

According to Shakil, the officers released his car on the condition that he would provide another Tk 500,000 the following day. However, AC Shariful retained his 14 mobile phones.

Akhtaruzzaman Shakil told Prothom Alo, “They frightened me by describing playing games as gambling and threatening to implicate me in a case, so I was forced to pay the money. I was even more frightened because the mobile phones contained my personal photos and videos. They demanded an iPhone in exchange for returning the mobile phones. They threatened to circulate the photos and videos on social media if I did not provide one.”

Shakil has a farm and runs a plastic-granule business in Khatunganj. He said he regularly plays games on his mobile phone.

The LIC branch of Chattogram Metropolitan Police operates under strict confidentiality. Its role is to gather intelligence using modern information technology to identify criminals and prevent crime.

The branch, located on the ground floor of the CMP office, has fingerprint-enabled doors, restricting entry to authorised personnel. Officers assigned to the branch also do not normally take part in regular operations.

The city police formed the investigation committee to verify the allegations and examine the roles of the officials concerned.

item.title: Govt unaware of EC’s announcement of UP election dates: Mir Shahe Alam
item.description:
State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Mir Shahe Alam has said that the government is unaware of the announcement of dates for the Union Parishad (UP) elections.

The state minister made the remarks while speaking to journalists at the Secretariat this morning, Tuesday.

Earlier, on Monday, Election Commissioner Abul Fazal Md Sanaullah said that the Union Parishad elections would be held in seven phases.

Mir Shahe Alam said the government knew nothing about the announcement of the dates for the UP elections. The Ministry of Local Government was also unaware of the matter.

He said there had been no correspondence between the government and the election commission on the issue, nor had there been any discussion through any other channel.

The state minister for local government also said the election commission is an independent body with constitutional authority to conduct elections.

In this regard, he said that, in accordance with established practice, the EC announces the dates of local government elections after discussions with the government. Preparatory meetings and law-and-order committee meetings are held, involving various matters, including the budget.

Mir Shahe Alam said there had been no discussion between the election commission and either the Ministry of Local Government or the government. “The government knows nothing about this,” he said.

The EC announced yesterday that the Union Parishad elections would be held in seven phases.

Speaking to journalists at the Nirbachan Bhaban in Agargaon, Election Commissioner Abul Fazal Md Sanaullah said the tentative date for the first phase of UP elections had been set for 12 November. Local government elections will begin with this phase.

The election commissioner further said the tentative dates for the subsequent phases are 13 December for the second phase, 30 December for the third, 17 January next year for the fourth, 4 February for the fifth, 22 April for the sixth, and 27 May for the seventh.

Earlier, in August this year, the election commission had announced a schedule and planned to begin the local government elections in October.

In June, in response to a question in parliament, the then local government minister had said that local government elections could begin gradually across the country from September or October, after the monsoon season. That, however, did not happen.

item.title: Gaibandha’s Haridas sent to jail after remand in flat fraud case
item.description:
Haridas Chandra Tarani Das, who had drawn attention for initiating the construction of an 81-foot-tall statue of Rama in Palashbari, Gaibandha, has been sent to jail after completing a two-day remand in a fraud case filed over an alleged embezzlement of nearly Tk 7.6 million (76 lakh) on the promise of providing a flat.

Police produced Haridas before the court on Monday after completing his remand and sought an order to keep him in jail. Following the plea, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Sarah Farzana Haque ordered that he be sent to jail.

Sub-Inspector Helal Uddin of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Prosecution Department confirmed the matter to Prothom Alo.

According to court sources, the court granted Haridas a two-day remand in the flat fraud case on 10 September.

Earlier, on 24 August, Mahbubur Rahman, an employee of a private organisation, filed the fraud case with Uttara West police station against Haridas Chandra Tarani Das and another man, Obaidul Islam.

According to the case statement, the accused took Tk 7,586,000 from complainant Mahbubur Rahman on the promise of providing him with a flat and allegedly embezzled the money.

Earlier, on 12 July, Sub-Inspector Saiful Islam of the CID’s Financial Crime Unit filed a case with Uttara West police station against Haridas and several others over an alleged money-laundering offence involving Tk 93.5 million (9.35 crore).

That same night, the Detective Branch (DB) of police arrested Haridas from an area near a temple in Palashbari upazila of Gaibandha. Following his remand in that case, the court sent him to jail on 16 July. He has remained in jail since then.

item.title: Mymensingh Medical College Hospital fire: 4 die, administration refutes reports of trampling incident
item.description:
Following a fire outbreak at Mymensingh Medical College Hospital, authorities confirmed four fatalities; however, the administration stated there is no evidence to suggest any deaths occurred as a result of being trampled.

Families of two of the deceased confirmed they died of natural causes, whilst the causes of death for the remaining two are yet to be determined, according to Mymensingh Divisional Commissioner SM Humayun Kabir.

Panic swept through patients and their relatives on Monday evening (14 September) after a fire broke out on the 7th floor of the hospital’s new building.

In the ensuing rush to evacuate down the stairwells, several individuals sustained injuries. Rumours subsequently circulated claiming six people had died after being trampled.

Divisional Commissioner SM Humayun Kabir and Abu Wahab Akanda Wahid, member of parliament for the Mymensingh-4 (Sadar) constituency, visited the hospital and addressed reporters at around 12:30 am.

The Divisional Commissioner stated, “We have found no evidence or data to support the claim that six people died after being trampled. We have interviewed the Fire Service personnel, emergency department physicians, nurses, and other staff members, and thoroughly examined their registers. There is no proof of any fatality caused by trampling.”

Addressing a list alleging five deaths, the Divisional Commissioner noted that one individual on that list remains alive and is receiving treatment in the hospital. Of the remaining four, the families of two have confirmed that their deaths were due to natural causes. Physicians are yet to provide a definitive cause of death for the other two, and further details will emerge following an investigation.

“We have not obtained any evidence to confirm any fatalities resulted directly from this event. Patients may pass away due to natural causes in a hospital setting; however, reports of deaths due to trampling are untrue,” he added.

Nevertheless, the Divisional Commissioner acknowledged that several individuals were injured in the scramble following the outbreak, suffering cuts or head injuries. Administration officials did not comment on whether any deaths were caused by smoke inhalation.

Responding to allegations regarding the crowd control bottleneck—caused by one of the hospital’s two stairwells being locked—the Commissioner stated they were aware of the issue. Hospital management explained that certain stairwells were locked for security reasons. Any administrative oversights will be thoroughly investigated.

Speaking earlier to newspersons, MP Abu Wahab Akanda, who also serves as Vice President of the hospital management committee, pointed out that the list of deceased included the name of an individual who is alive and currently undergoing medical treatment.

He urged journalists to verify the patient's condition against the list.

“A patient named Jahanara, listed among the deceased, is alive and undergoing treatment. A quick cross-check between the list and reality will clarify the matter,” the MP said.

Conversely, relatives of two patients claimed that their loved ones died after falling down the stairs during the panic. The deceased have been identified as Kulsum Akhtar, 35, wife of Shahidul Islam from Balikha village in Tarakanda, and Shahajahan Monir, 45, from Bishnurampur village in Phulpur's Rangamatia Union.

At around midnight on Monday, Nazma Akhtar, the sister-in-law of Kulsum Akhtar, told Prothom Alo that Kulsum had been staying in Ward 31 (Pediatrics) for the past 12 days caring for her 12-year-old son, Swadhin, who was suffering from jaundice. Kulsum was accompanied by her 18-year-old daughter, Mim.

Describing the incident, Nazma stated that as panic spread, Kulsum attempted to navigate her children down the stairwell. Mim managed to exit first. Upon returning, she found bystanders pulling her brother Swadhin out, but her mother was missing.

According to Nazma, Kulsum was subsequently recovered and placed on oxygen assistance. She was breathing at the time, but died shortly before Nazma arrived at the hospital. “We have grievances regarding this,” Nazma said, adding that the family had taken the body home after obtaining the necessary paperwork from the hospital.

In another instance, Shahajahan Monir had been receiving treatment for tuberculosis on the third floor of the new building for approximately 10 to 12 days.

His son, Palash Molla, stated that during the fire, his father, mother Harisa Akhtar, and aunt Jahanara Akhtar were attempting to descend the stairs together when they were knocked down by the rushing crowd behind them. His mother and aunt were subsequently admitted to Ward 10 with injuries.

Palash mentioned he was not present at the hospital during the incident and visited his mother later. Relatives have taken his father’s body back to their village, and he was shown photographs of the body via mobile phone.

Purna Chandra Mutsuddi, Assistant Director of Mymensingh Fire Service, stated that they received the fire alarm at 5:55 pm. Firefighters arrived within 10 minutes, deploying 10 units to combat the blaze. The fire was brought fully under control by 6:30 pm.

He further noted that preliminary assessments suggest the fire originated from electrical overheating in a circuit board within the control room of an elevator on the 7th floor of the new building. The exact cause will be confirmed following a formal investigation.

item.title: Three-way mayoral contest takes shape in Dhaka
item.description:
The candidates of three political parties for the elections to Dhaka’s two city corporations have largely been finalised. National Citizen Party (NCP) has already announced Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain as its candidate for Dhaka North and Nasiruddin Patwari for Dhaka South.

BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami have yet to announce their candidates, but their probable candidates for the two city corporations are also said to have been largely finalised. Both parties are carrying out their activities strategically.

As this year’s local government elections will be non-partisan, BNP and Jamaat will not announce candidates directly. Instead, they will select candidates and extend their support to them. Thus, although there will be no party symbols on the ballot, the support of the BNP and Jamaat will be important in the electoral contest.

Senior BNP sources said the party had almost finalised Safiqul Islam Khan for the mayoral post in Dhaka North and Abdus Salam for Dhaka South. A notification issued by the Local Government Division on 22 February appointed the two as administrators of the respective city corporations.

According to party sources, when they were appointed as administrators, they were instructed to prepare for the city corporation elections alongside providing civic services. As a result, although BNP has not formally announced its support, there is little uncertainty within the party over its preferred candidates for the two city corporations.

Abdus Salam, administrator of Dhaka South City Corporation, told Prothom Alo yesterday, Monday, “Before I took charge, Dhaka South City Corporation had become virtually inactive. That situation has changed considerably. I am trying to ensure that citizens receive the services and facilities they need.”

Saying that he was preparing both for the election and for providing civic services, Abdus Salam said, “I am trying to work according to what the people want. Through this, I am preparing for the election.”

A responsible BNP leader, however, said that the two candidates were currently in place, but it was difficult to say what would happen in the end. There would certainly be surveys through various channels as part of the candidate-selection process, he said.

Jamaat’s candidates also almost finalised

The preferred candidates of the main opposition party, Jamaat-e-Islami, for the two Dhaka city corporations have also largely been settled. The party is expected to support Mohammad Selim Uddin in Dhaka North and Md Abu Shadik (Shadik Kayem) in Dhaka South. Selim Uddin is the ameer of Jamaat’s Dhaka North city unit, while Shadik Kayem is vice-president of the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (DUCSU). Until July, he was the central secretary for international affairs of Islami Chhatra Shibir. He is currently an associate member of Jamaat.

Selim Uddin previously contested the parliamentary election from Sylhet-6 (Golapganj–Beanibazar) and was defeated. Shadik Kayem, meanwhile, is primarily known electorally for his involvement in student politics at DUCSU.

For some time, Selim Uddin has been conducting organisational and welfare activities in various parts of Dhaka North. Shadik Kayem is also taking part in Jamaat’s internal programmes and carrying out activities as a potential candidate.

A responsible Jamaat-e-Islami leader told Prothom Alo that since Shadik Kayem still represents DUCSU, his active involvement with Jamaat is therefore not being made public.

Jamaat Central Majlis-e-Shura member Md Ataur Rahman Sarker told Prothom Alo, “Mohammad Selim Uddin has been reaching out to people from various professions and walks of life, and he is receiving a very positive response. We are hopeful that city residents will elect him and help move forward towards fulfilling their aspirations.”

Jamaat Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar spoke about the matter yesterday in Dhaka in response to questions from journalists after a party event. He said the party was organisationally preparing for the local government elections.

The process of nominating candidates for union, upazila, district and city corporation elections was at its final stage, he said. Candidates had also been selected for the two Dhaka city corporations, although they had not yet been formally announced.

Referring to media reports, he said Selim Uddin and Shadik Kayem were the party’s candidates for Dhaka North and South respectively.

Asif faces first election, Patwary returns to the electoral field

The NCP has directly announced candidates for both city corporations. Last Sunday, party convener Nahid Islam announced Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain for Dhaka North and Nasiruddin Patwary for Dhaka South.

This will be Asif Mahmud’s first test in electoral politics. He has never contested an election at either the parliamentary or local government level. Nasir Uddin Patwary, on the other hand, has experience of contesting a national election. He contested the Dhaka-8 constituency against senior BNP leader Mirza Abbas and was defeated.

Ahead of the city corporation elections, both Asif Mahmud and Nasiruddin Patwary changed their voter constituencies. Asif became a voter in Ward 37 of Dhaka North, while Patwary became a voter in Ward 21 of Dhaka South. They were announced as candidates for the two city corporations shortly afterward.

Three parties, three types of candidates

Political observers say the BNP is putting forward two candidates with experience in city administration. Jamaat’s North candidate is a leader of its city organisation, while its South candidate is a familiar face from student politics.

The BNP’s South candidate, Abdus Salam, is also an experienced organiser. He was one of the senior leaders of the party’s Dhaka South city unit for a long time and also served as acting mayor of the city corporation. He is currently a member of the BNP chairman’s Advisory Council.

The North candidate, Safiqul Islam Khan, is a central vice-president of Jubo Dal. In the last parliamentary election, he contested Dhaka-15 as the BNP candidate and was defeated by Jamaat ameer Shafiqur Rahman. The NCP, meanwhile, has chosen two prominent figures from the front line of the political change brought about by the July mass uprising.

BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi told Prothom Alo yesterday that the BNP would not nominate any candidate. However, the grassroots have been instructed to vote collectively for whoever is locally popular and acceptable, and ensure that person’s victory.

People familiar with the matter believe that because the elections will be non-partisan and there will be no party symbols on the ballot, candidates’ personal identities and acceptability will become important. At the same time, a major question will be how much the support of the BNP and Jamaat influences the vote.

The elections to Dhaka’s two city corporations could therefore also serve as a test of the popularity of the three political forces. Whether voters are more drawn to administrative experience, party organisation or a new political identity will become clear in the election.

item.title: In frames: Workers toil at a wholesale vegetable market
item.description:
The hustle and bustle of workers at the wholesale vegetable market begins at the crack of dawn. One truck after another pulls in, and the workers unload sacks of vegetables and arrange them at the market. They are paid according to the weight of the sacks they carry. From morning until evening, they work relentlessly, lifting heavy sacks onto their shoulders and, at times, carrying them on their heads.

More than 150 workers are involved in loading and unloading vegetables at this market. After a full day of hard labour, a worker earns an average of Tk1,000 to Tk1,200. That income is what keeps their families going. While shoppers at the market see only the buying and selling of vegetables, for these workers every sack represents another day of keeping their families’ livelihoods afloat.
