item.title: Kobir: BIMSTEC must look beyond tensions, widen regional engagement
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir has urged BIMSTEC member states to look beyond bilateral tensions and widen regional engagement, stressing mutual trust, political will and a shared sense of purpose to make the grouping more effective.
"For BIMSTEC to be successful, we must not dwell on bilateral tensions but widen the net of engagement," he said.
The state minister was speaking at a reception hosted by BIMSTEC Secretary General Indra Mani Pandey and his spouse Sushma Pandey at a hotel in Dhaka, marking BIMSTEC Secretariat Establishment Day on Monday evening.
Diplomats, including representatives from BIMSTEC member states, business leaders, civil society representatives and senior journalists attended the reception.
Kobir said Bangladesh would work closely with all member states and the BIMSTEC Secretariat in the coming months to advance implementation across various mechanisms and prepare for the next BIMSTEC Summit, which Bangladesh is expected to host in Dhaka in 2027.
The summit of heads of state and government in Dhaka would provide an important opportunity to review progress, set new priorities and give further political direction to the common regional agenda, he said.
"I am confident that BIMSTEC can become an even more dynamic bridge between South and Southeast Asia and a strong force for regional peace, progress, and sustainable development," Kobir said.
On behalf of the government and people of Bangladesh, he extended warm felicitations to the governments and peoples of all BIMSTEC member states on the occasion.
"Let us not walk out of regional cooperation regardless of differences. We must have the tenacity. We must have the vision to digest difficult challenges, difficult tensions, and difficult dialogue to make regional cooperation a success with mutual trust, political will, and a shared sense of purpose," he said.
He also appreciated the BIMSTEC secretary general and his team for their steadfast commitment and continued service to the shared regional endeavour.
Kobir said the establishment of the BIMSTEC Secretariat in Dhaka 12 years ago was a defining step in the institutional development of the regional grouping.
Over the past 12 years, he said, the Secretariat had evolved into the central coordinating hub of BIMSTEC, supporting member states, facilitating sectoral cooperation, preserving institutional continuity and helping translate decisions of leaders and ministers into practical programmes.
"Bangladesh is proud to host this regional institution and remains committed to providing the support necessary for it to discharge its responsibilities effectively," he said.
The state minister said the Bay of Bengal had connected the peoples of South and Southeast Asia for centuries, long before the emergence of modern regionalism.
"This Bay carried culture, knowledge, faith, and human interaction between South and Southeast Asia. BIMSTEC gives contemporary institutional form to those historic connections," he said.
The seven BIMSTEC member states - Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand - together represent a vast pool of people, resources, talent and economic potential, he said.
"Our task is to transform this shared geography into shared prosperity," Kobir said.
He noted that economic uncertainty, fragmented supply chains, climate change, energy insecurity, public health risks, cyber threats, transnational crime and humanitarian challenges did not respect national borders.
"No country can address them effectively in isolation. A stronger BIMSTEC is therefore not simply desirable; it is a strategic necessity for the peace, resilience, and prosperity of our region," he said.
Bangladesh assumed the BIMSTEC chairmanship with a clear commitment to making the organisation more functional, visible, inclusive and, importantly, people-centred, he said.
"Our approach is guided by practical cooperation and measurable outcomes," he said.
As the lead country for trade, investment and development, including the blue economy, Bangladesh attached particular importance to strengthening regional economic integration, expanding connectivity, promoting sustainable use of marine resources and creating opportunities for businesses and people, Kobir said.
He said progress towards the BIMSTEC Free Trade Area remained essential.
Kobir also highlighted the blue economy, describing the Bay of Bengal as one of the region's greatest shared assets.
Its fisheries, shipping routes, renewable energy prospects, marine biodiversity, tourism potential and coastal livelihoods could become drivers of sustainable growth, he said.
"Connectivity must remain at the heart of the BIMSTEC project," Kobir said, stressing the need for sustained implementation, innovative financing and stronger engagement with the private sector and development partners.
He said prosperity must rest on the foundation of peace and security, making cooperation in counterterrorism, transnational crime, human trafficking, narcotics, cybersecurity, disaster management and maritime security indispensable.
"We must develop trust and strengthen our cooperation further," he said.
Kobir also underscored the importance of people-to-people connectivity through tourism, education, culture, youth exchanges, professional networks, think-tank cooperation, innovation and greater interaction among the private sectors.
"BIMSTEC must become not only an intergovernmental process but also a living regional community," he said.
As the current chair of BIMSTEC and host country of the BIMSTEC Secretariat, Bangladesh's responsibility extended beyond convening meetings, he said.
He said Bangladesh would work with all member states and the Secretariat to advance implementation and prepare for the 2027 summit in Dhaka.
"Regional instruments like BIMSTEC can work as diplomatic enablers for regional engagement and cooperation," Kobir said.

item.title: Families of 2 soldiers killed in Hathazari accident receive aid from PM
item.description:
Family members of two soldiers who were killed in an accident during a field firing exercise in Chittagong's Hathazari, met Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Tuesday and received financial assistance from him.
The meeting took place at the Prime Minister’s Office in Tejgaon in the morning, where Tarique spoke to the family members and expressed his deep condolences over the deaths.
“The soldiers lost their lives while performing their duties for the country. They have been martyred while serving the country. The nation will remember their sacrifice with deep respect,” he said.
The prime minister assured the bereaved families that the government and the Bangladesh Army would always stand by them and provide necessary support.
“The government and the Army will always stand by your families. Along with providing necessary assistance, the government will also fulfil its responsibility to look after the families of the martyred soldiers,” he added.
The prime minister later handed over cheques for financial assistance to the families of the two soldiers.
The Army also announced plans to build a house for each family at the soldiers’ permanent addresses.
Arrangements will also be made to provide jobs to their wives and monthly allowances for their children.
The two soldiers — Sainik (Operator) Abu Bakar Siddique and Sainik (Gunner) Md Tasnim Rifat — were killed in a shell explosion during tank firing at the Hathazari Field Firing Range on September 9.
Tarique’s wife Dr Zubaida Rahman, Chief of Army Staff General Waker-Uz-Zaman and senior Army officers were present during the meeting.
Members of Abu Bakar Siddique’s family who met the prime minister were his wife Suraiya Akter Juthi, daughter Fatema Siddika, father Abdul Wahab and mother Parvin Akter.
Members of Md Tasnim Rifat’s family included his wife Mosammat Fahmida Afrin, daughter Rafsa Tasnim Ifra and father Md Asadul Haque.

item.title: US Supreme Court blocks Trump mail-in ballot restrictions
item.description:
The US Supreme Court dealt a major blow Monday to President Donald Trump's attempts to restrict mail-in voting before the November midterm elections, denying his request to lift an order halting the divisive plan.
Only two of the six conservative justices on the nine-member panel offered a dissent.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in a concurring opinion with the majority, said Trump's plan may ultimately be legal in the long run, but "state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."
Several states, including North Carolina, have already begun sending mail-in ballots to voters.
Trump signed an executive order in March seeking to restrict mail-in voting, saying without evidence that it is vulnerable to fraud. The order quickly prompted multiple legal challenges.
Democratic-led states sued the administration on grounds that under the US Constitution, states -- and not the federal government -- retain broad control over the administration of elections.
Trump's executive order would require the compilation of lists of eligible voters and for the US Postal Service (USPS) to deliver ballots only to voters who are on the lists.
The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) hailed the Supreme Court's decision as a "major win for voting rights, election integrity, and democracy."
"This administration keeps testing the limits of its power, as if the rules governing our elections are merely suggestions to ignore when they don't suit the president's agenda," said Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the ACLU Voting Rights Project.
"The president does not run our elections, the Postal Service does not get to decide whose ballot counts, and voters -- not the White House -- will decide November's elections."
Officials from several states had warned that a lack of legal clarity around the plan was sowing chaos months before the November 3 vote.
A USPS whistleblower had also warned that millions of Americans may not receive ballots because the systems being used by the postal service have been put together in a "sloppy and rushed manner."
Trump has long been a critic of mail-in ballots but has frequently used them himself, including when he voted by mail in Florida's Republican primary earlier this year.
The president has for years claimed without evidence that mail-in voting is highly vulnerable to fraud, repeatedly linking it to his false assertion that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him by Democrat Joe Biden.
Polls show that Trump's Republican Party faces a serious threat of losing its narrow control of Congress in November, particularly the House of Representatives.
If Democrats win, they have signaled they would block Trump's agenda and could even move to impeach him for the third time.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 13th among world's most polluted cities
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 13th among the world's most polluted cities on Tuesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 101 at 10:37 am.
According to the AQI scale, the city's air quality was classified as “Unhealthy for sensitive groups,” indicating that vulnerable people may face minor health risks.
Malaysia's Kuala Lumpur topped the global pollution list with an AQI score of 205.
Kinshasa of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City ranked second and third, respectively, with AQI scores of 167 and 165.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’, 151 to 200 ‘unhealthy’, 201 to 300 ‘very unhealthy’, while levels above 301 are deemed ‘hazardous’, posing serious health risks.
The AQI, which provides daily updates on air quality, indicates how clean or polluted the air is and highlights potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically worsening in winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly due to stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Probe body formed over Mymensingh hospital fire
item.description:
A five-member investigation committee has been formed following reports that six people died in a stampede after a fire broke out in a lift at the new building of Mymensingh Medical College Hospital.
Professor Golam Rahman of the hospital’s Department of Medicine will head the committee.
The other members are hospital Assistant Director (Administration) Dr Mainuddin Khan, an assistant director of the Fire Service, an executive engineer of the Public Works Department (PWD), and a PWD electrical engineer.
The hospital authorities formed the committee on Tuesday morning and asked it to submit its report within three working days.
A fire broke out in a lift under construction at the hospital’s new building on Monday evening. Several people were injured while rushing down the stairs following the incident.
Reports later spread through the media and social media that six people, including a child, had died in the incident.
Senior administrative officials visited the hospital later that night and held a closed-door meeting.
Although four deaths were reported following the fire, authorities found no evidence that any of the victims died in a stampede.
Two of the victims died of natural causes, their families confirmed, while the causes of death of the other two remain unclear, Mymensingh Divisional Commissioner SM Humayun Kabir said.

item.title: US judge postpones new visa rules for foreign students, journalists
item.description:
A US federal judge on Monday postponed implementation of a Trump administration policy that would impose stricter limits on how long foreign students and journalists can study or work in the United States.
The preliminary injunction from District Judge Dennis Saylor came one day before the new visa rules from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) were scheduled to take effect.
Under the proposed new rules, foreigners on student visas would be admitted for a maximum of up to four years, after which they would have to apply for an extension. International students were previously allowed to remain for the duration of their studies.
Foreign journalists would be limited to stays of just 240 days, or around eight months, but could apply for extensions of similar duration. Until now they could stay up to five years.
Chinese journalists would get just 90 days, with extensions of 90 days.
A coalition of unions representing universities, teachers and journalists had filed a lawsuit challenging the visa restrictions.
Saylor put implementation of the new DHS rules on hold for now without ruling on the merits of the case and scheduled another hearing for October 2.
But in an accompanying memo, the judge expressed skepticism about the visa restrictions on international students and journalists.
He said the current system has permitted tens of millions of foreign students to come to the United States, resulting in "groundbreaking research in science, medicine, and technology, substantial economic growth, and a host of other benefits."
"Rather than attempt to improve that system, DHS elected to replace it with a new program that will substantially restrict the overall number of foreign students, researchers, professors, and journalists," he said.
The judge said that under the new rules, DHS denials of visa extensions would be "entirely discretionary and unappealable."
"A DHS official -- based on limited and vague criteria, and with no possibility of appeal -- will have the power to cut short the academic, research, or teaching activities of any non-US citizen for no reason or any reason."
Foreign journalists applying for visa extensions would also have "no recourse and no appeal" in the event they are turned down, Saylor said.
"The possibilities for abuse are rampant -- in particular, the obvious likelihood that the visas of foreign journalists who are critical of the government (or, more particularly, DHS officials) will not be renewed," he said.
When it proposed the rule, DHS cited national security grounds, an argument the judge said "borders on the absurd" and was "based almost entirely on a small handful of anecdotes."
The visa restrictions are part of a broader immigration crackdown by President Donald Trump spanning aggressive enforcement operations in major cities as well as new restrictions on legal pathways to citizenship.
The United States welcomed more than 1.1 million international students in the 2023-24 academic year, more than any other country, according to official data.

item.title: Beyond cost and capacity
item.description:
Bangladesh’s apparel industry is one of the country’s greatest economic success stories. In FY2024–25, apparel exports reached approximately $39.35 billion, including roughly $7.55bn to the United States alone. Europe remains an even larger market, with the EU continuing to be the most important destination for Bangladeshi apparel.
Those numbers demonstrate something important: Bangladesh already knows how to manufacture for the world.
But the question for the next decade is different. Manufacturing excellence is no longer enough.
Bangladesh has built its position through cost competitiveness, manufacturing capacity, compliance, and long-standing buyer relationships. These advantages remain enormously important.
But the competitive environment is becoming harder.
Tariff uncertainty in the United States, energy and gas constraints at home, financing pressures, and periods of political and social instability all create risks for manufacturers. At the same time, competitors such as Vietnam continue to strengthen their position.
Much of this is outside an individual company's control.
A manufacturer cannot determine US trade policy. It cannot single-handedly solve Bangladesh's energy infrastructure or broader political environment.
But there is one significant lever companies can control: How effectively they find, engage, convert, and grow customers.
That is where modern B2B marketing becomes a commercial capability rather than a communications exercise.
In traditional B2B environments, marketing is sometimes treated as corporate communications: A website, brochures, trade fairs, factory videos, and perhaps some social media.
Modern B2B marketing goes considerably further.
A potential North American buyer may research suppliers online long before speaking with a salesperson. They may search Google, visit a manufacturer's website, review its LinkedIn presence, examine certifications and sustainability credentials, assess capabilities, and compare several suppliers before anyone knows they are looking.
That changes what a manufacturer's digital presence needs to accomplish.
A website should answer commercial questions: What categories does the company specialize in? What makes its manufacturing capability different? Which markets does it serve? What are its sustainability credentials? What innovation can it offer? Why should a buyer initiate a conversation?
Then comes the machinery behind it: SEO and keyword strategy, thought-leadership content, case studies, product and capability demonstrations, strong calls-to-action, and lead capture.
Marketing can therefore become a meaningful contributor to sales. For the right organization, I would argue that a well-designed marketing engine should aspire to generate or influence 20% or more of the sales pipeline, rather than being measured primarily by impressions, website traffic, or event attendance.
There is a market beyond the largest global buyers
The biggest international retailers and apparel companies already have sophisticated sourcing organizations and established supplier networks. Digital marketing will not suddenly replace those relationships.
But that is not the entire addressable market.
Across North America and Europe, there are thousands of mid-sized retailers, emerging brands, e-commerce businesses, specialist labels, and growing companies without the sourcing infrastructure of the world's largest brands.
This is where discoverability matters.
Bangladeshi manufacturers can identify companies matching their production strengths, understand their growth and buying signals, map relevant decision-makers, and develop targeted account-based marketing programs.
Instead of waiting for the next buyer to find Bangladesh, why not systematically identify the next 500 potential buyers?
Customer acquisition is only half the opportunity.
Consider a manufacturer with 20 established international buyers. How systematically are those relationships being nurtured outside the normal sales and merchandising process?
A quarterly buyer newsletter could communicate new capabilities, sustainability investments, machinery, available capacity, innovation, product development, and relevant market insights.
A buyer sourcing one category may not even know that the same manufacturer has developed significant capabilities in another.
This is lifecycle marketing: Using structured communication to deepen relationships, increase retention, and expand share of wallet.
The same principle applies to LinkedIn. Senior executives in Bangladesh's apparel industry possess enormous knowledge, but much of it remains invisible internationally.
Writing intelligently about sourcing trends, sustainability, materials, manufacturing innovation, or supply-chain developments builds authority.
Webinars can do the same. Imagine a manufacturer hosting a useful discussion for overseas buyers on changing sourcing economics or AI in apparel supply chains.
That is not vanity marketing. It is commercial credibility.
This is where the opportunity becomes particularly interesting.
AI agents can already help businesses conduct market research, identify target accounts, analyze competitors, map decision-makers, monitor buying signals, personalize outreach, and enrich CRM data.
Instead of asking a salesperson to manually research hundreds of potential customers, an AI-enabled system can screen thousands of businesses and help prioritize the accounts most likely to fit a manufacturer's capabilities.
AI can also extend beyond marketing and sales.
Historical orders, seasonality, buyer behaviour, and market signals can increasingly support demand forecasting, inventory management, and production planning. Market-intelligence work that once required weeks can sometimes be compressed dramatically.
The objective should not be replacing people. It should be giving good people better intelligence, greater productivity, and faster decision-making.
There is also a human problem worth acknowledging.
When an industry has generated significant wealth for decades, success itself can create a comfort zone.
If relationships, manufacturing capacity and cost competitiveness have worked extremely well, the natural question is: Why change?
Because the customer is changing.
North American and European businesses increasingly operate in sophisticated, data-driven commercial environments.
Their marketing organizations use CRM platforms, automation, analytics, content, account-based marketing, intent data, and now AI.
If the customers we want to sell to are becoming more sophisticated, our methods of reaching and serving them must evolve as well.
Bangladesh should not abandon what made its apparel industry successful. It should build another layer on top of it.
Manufacturing excellence plus commercial intelligence.
Relationships plus data.
Sales plus lifecycle marketing.
Experience plus AI.
And capacity plus a compelling global presence.
Technology will disrupt industries. Trade relationships will change. New competitors will emerge. But apparel has one extraordinary characteristic: Clothing is a basic human need.
As long as there are people, there will be demand for clothing. The strategic question is therefore not whether this market will exist. It is how much of the future market Bangladesh will capture.
We have already demonstrated that Bangladesh can manufacture for the world. The next opportunity is to become equally world-class at finding the market, understanding the buyer, communicating our value, and systematically creating demand.
Nawrin Sultana is a Bangladeshi-Canadian marketing consultant, blending her cultural roots with a global perspective. Email: nawrin.sultana@gmail.com .

item.title: Ensuring education for all
item.description:
The declining enrolment in government primary schools in Dhaka is a truly unfortunate situation that must be rectified.
These institutions remain an important avenue for affordable education, particularly for lower-income families, yet many are struggling with empty classrooms, poor infrastructure, inadequate facilities, and concerns over the quality and regularity of teaching.
A particularly troubling, recurring scenario has been observed at several of these schools recently, including one with only a handful out of over 50 recorded students present in one classroom.
Similar discrepancies were found elsewhere, alongside waterlogging, unclean surroundings, ageing buildings, and limited space for children -- all dire conditions that inevitably push parents towards private institutions.
This observation comes at a time when the government has rightly stressed that no child should be deprived of education because of financial hardship.
Continued welfare programs, educational materials, and other assistance for disadvantaged children are certainly a positive step in the right direction. The emphasis on quality education and necessary facilities is also welcome.
But ensuring access to education means little if the public institutions providing that access are allowed to deteriorate.
Financial assistance can help families send children to school, but the schools themselves must offer a safe, clean, and effective learning environment.
The problem is clearly too widespread to be countered through isolated interventions. Rigorous measures are pivotal, beginning with accurate enrolment and attendance data, regular physical inspections, infrastructure repairs, and stronger accountability for teachers and administrators.
The government must also listen closely to parents and students and understand why they are choosing to skip school.
Modernizing school buildings, as the authorities have pledged, is welcome, but it must be accompanied by improvements in teaching, monitoring, safety, and student engagement.
Government primary schools should be places parents and pupils actively choose, not institutions they turn away from. Restoring public confidence will require sustained commitment and, above all, action that results in a greater, more sustained turnout in the classroom.

item.title: A meeting that should faze us
item.description:
On Sunday, a high-level Chevron delegation called on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Secretariat. The two sides discussed investment in Bangladesh's existing gas fields and the exploration of new ones.
State media described it as a productive courtesy call. It was. But it is also worth reading for what it quietly reveals.
Chevron already produces roughly half of Bangladesh's domestic natural gas from fields -- Bibiyana, Jalalabad -- that have anchored the national supply for two decades.
That a government facing the worst energy crisis in a generation must now ask this same company, warmly, to look for more, says something about how the last three decades were spent.
A gas-dependent country cannot indefinitely defer the one task that matters most: Exploring for its own gas.
The numbers make the point on their own. Since 1998, Bangladesh has drilled on the order of 100 exploration wells. India drilled 545 in a single year. Bangladesh's own scientists have said for years that the country remains among the least explored of the world's promising gas basins, and that each new discovery raises the odds of finding the next one nearby.
Part of the shortfall is capacity, not just will: BAPEX, Bangladesh's state exploration company, has neither the rig fleet nor the seismic and drilling budget to explore the country's remaining prospective basins on its own, and was never resourced to.
Where domestic capacity is this constrained, the honest response is to widen the field -- inviting international exploration companies, under transparent production-sharing terms, into blocks BAPEX cannot reach alone, rather than treating exploration as a task for one state company operating far below the scale the country's geology demands.
Instead, for years, the money that might have expanded that capacity went to subsidizing LNG cargoes bought to cover the gap that under-exploration created.
The human cost of that choice now has an address: Ashuganj, Brahmanbaria. The state-owned fertilizer factory there once ran around the clock, employed more than 1,200 people, and produced over 1,000 tons of urea a day for a country of 170 million that depends on it to grow food.
It has sat idle since March 2025 -- 18 months now -- because there is no gas to run it.
It is not alone. Of the five major urea plants under the Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation, four were shut down this year for the same reason; only one remains intermittently operational, and officials do not expect it to last.
A country that cannot keep its own fertilizer plants running is not managing an inconvenience. It is confronting a threat to food security that deserves to be treated as such.
None of this means Chevron's investment isn't welcome, or that Sunday's meeting was the wrong move.
Expanding output at mature, already-producing fields is sensible and overdue, and it can happen faster than new exploration can.
But there is a difference between welcoming a partner's investment and depending on that partner more than a country should, and Bangladesh's own recent history is a useful caution here.
We have seen what happens when Bangladesh lets a single external actor set the terms of its energy supply on opaque terms: The Adani Godda contract, signed without public disclosure, now embeds a price roughly 40-80% above what comparable power costs on India's own exchange, into every electricity bill in the country.
Chevron's relationship with Bangladesh is a different and considerably healthier one -- three decades of transparent production-sharing agreements, not a bilateral contract negotiated out of public view -- and that distinction matters.
Even so, the broader lesson holds: A country that builds its own exploration and negotiating capacity chooses its partnerships from a position of strength. A country that does not will keep finding itself, respectfully, asking.
The government's own five-point plan, announced in September, gets the direction right: Expand domestic production, strengthen BAPEX, drill 106 new wells, and open the door to outside exploration expertise where domestic capacity falls short.
The Chevron meeting is a welcome down payment on the near-term half of that plan -- the mature fields that can produce faster. It should not become a substitute for the harder half: The seismic surveys, the BAPEX budget, and the wider invitation to international exploration partners that the twelve-year reserve clock now makes urgent rather than optional.
The family in Brahmanbaria who watched Ashuganj go quiet did not choose LNG subsidies over BAPEX funding, did not sign the Adani contract, and did not decide, year after year, that exploration could wait.
They are simply the ones living with those choices now, in lost wages and strained food security.
A courtesy call at the Secretariat is a welcome step, but it is not itself the solution. That will require a government prepared to fund exploration, and to open the field to those who can help expand it, as if the twelve-year reserve clock were real -- because it is.
Ahad Chowdhury, PhD, is a geologist and environmental scientist based in Louisville, Kentucky, USA.

item.title: Making public service more grounded
item.description:
The government’s decision to drop honorifics such as “Excellency” and “Honourable” from official communications is commendable and a step towards making public service more grounded and representative of the people it is meant to serve.
The directive, which applies to the president, prime minister, ministers, state ministers, and deputy ministers, is effective immediately across government offices.
Titles and formalities have had their place in official settings, but excessive deference can sometimes reinforce an unnecessary distance between those who govern and those who are governed.
Public office is a responsibility, not a position that should require elaborate displays of reverence, and removing such honorifics sends a useful symbolic message: Those who hold office are, ultimately, servants of the state and its people.
This is particularly important as Bangladesh continues to work towards strengthening institutions and building greater public trust.
A culture of accountability begins with recognizing that authority comes with obligations. Officials must be accessible, responsive, and answerable for their decisions, rather than being placed on a pedestal through language and ceremony.
Of course, changing forms of address alone will not transform the culture of governance. The significance of this decision will depend on whether it is accompanied by meaningful changes in how public institutions operate.
Respect for citizens must be reflected in efficient services, transparency, responsible decision-making, and accountability at every level of government.
It is, therefore, important that this commendable move does not remain merely symbolic. The same spirit should inform wider administrative reforms, ensuring that public servants remember the purpose of the positions they hold.
A government exists to serve its citizens, and the language used by its institutions should reflect that principle. Moving away from unnecessary honorifics is a small but welcome step towards a more modest, accessible, and people-centred culture of governance.
We hope it will be followed by actions that make public service worthy of the trust placed in it.

item.title: Asian Games set for liftoff but will everyone have a bed?
item.description:
The Asian Games open in Japan on Saturday with 2028 Olympics places up for grabs, fast-rising talents of world sport in action and thousands of athletes staying on a cruise ship in typhoon season.
More than 17,000 competitors and officials are expected at the continent's biggest sporting spectacular, which takes place in Nagoya and the wider Aichi prefecture until October 4.
The number of participants -- more than the Olympics -- has been a sore point for stretched-to-the-limit organisers, who initially expected 15,000 and have had to scramble to find accommodation for the rest.
They opted from the start to house athletes in temporary accommodation in a bid to cut costs, ranging from a cruise liner and wooden containers to hotel rooms.
Organisers say that the 20th edition of the Games, which were first held in 1951, will be "the most spectacular for generations".
Between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes and officials will stay on the Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which usually features 571 cabins, seven swimming pools, eight restaurants and nine bars.
Cruise ships have been used previously as accommodation at international sporting events, but never on this scale.
The unusual accommodation plans have been met with concern by some countries, with India even building their own replica container huts to prepare athletes for their stay.
On Monday, South Korean sports officials branded the facilities as "the worst" accommodation ever at the Games and said the beds were too short.
With just days to go, a Korean Olympic committee official also told AFP that there was "a serious shortage of accommodation".
- Rain, go away -
Organisers are adamant that everyone will have a bed and confident that the typhoon season that usually visits Japan in September and October will not dampen the party.
Weather has already disrupted preparations, with record rainfall forcing athletes to evacuate their accommodation briefly last week.
Rainwater also seeped into some competition venues, although organisers said there was no serious damage. More rain is forecast this week.
Athletes from 45 countries and territories will compete in more than 40 sports across the two weeks.
Basketball and football are already under way, with several more events set to start before Saturday's glittering opening ceremony.
As always at the Asian Games, Olympics staples such as athletics and swimming will sit side-by-side with regional favourites like sepak takraw and kabaddi.
In a bid to attract younger viewers there will be eSports, breakdancing and BMX cycling.
Padel, the fast-growing racquet sport, and MMA will make their Asian Games debuts.
The Games will function as qualifiers for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics in seven sports including surfing, tennis, archery and squash.
Among those competing will be Philippine tennis sensation Alexandra Eala and a pair of prodigies in 15-year-old Indian cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi.
"I love playing and competing with the Philippine team," said Eala, who is skipping the China Open to take part.
- Gold rush -
Taiwan boxer Lin Yu-ting will also be there, two years after she won Paris Olympics gold in the middle of a major gender row that saw her eligibility questioned.
Hosts Japan will look to their Olympic champions for success, with gymnast Shinnosuke Oka and javelin thrower Haruka Kitaguchi named in their team.
North Korea will have more than 100 athletes competing across 14 sports, aiming to "bring joy to Marshal Kim Jong Un".
China will again expect to top the medals table after winning a whopping 201 golds and 383 medals on home soil in Hangzhou at the Covid-delayed Games in 2023.
They will send more than 800 athletes, including 36 Olympic champions.
"We will showcase China's standard and strength on the regional and global stage," said diver Wang Zongyuan.
Sooryavanshi will be part of an India cricket team looking to make a statement before the sport returns to the Olympics in LA after an absence of 128 years.
India could face bitter rivals Pakistan in the final at Nagoya's new purpose-built cricket ground.
Reports of tents serving as dressing rooms and distant washroom facilities have left some of the top teams unimpressed.

item.title: Leeds thrash Newcastle to go third in the Premier League
item.description:
Leeds demolished Newcastle 4-1 to climb up to third in the Premier League table on Monday and inflict a punishing first defeat for Magpies boss Matthias Jaissle.
A Lewis Miley own goal opened the floodgates before Jayden Bogle, Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Noah Okafor completed the rout at Elland Road.
Newcastle had made a positive start under Jaissle despite the upheaval of losing manager Eddie Howe and key players Anthony Gordon, Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali in the off-season.
Despite being owned by the financial might of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, Newcastle targeted rising stars to fill the void of those that left and were outmuscled by a more experienced Leeds.
"It was clear from the start and I said that many times that we will have up and downs, challenges along the way," said Jaissle. "We faced that challenge and it's tough, it's really tough."
A bad night for the visitors began inside the first 20 minutes when Nico Gonzalez had to be replaced as a concussion substitute.
That left 18-year-old Sean Steur and Lewis Miley, 20, together at the heart of the Newcastle midfield and the later unfortunately had the final touch after Ao Tanaka's strike took two deflections before looping into the net.
The visitors failed to regain their composure as just two minutes later Leeds doubled their advantage.
Calvert-Lewin rose highest to meet James Justin's cross but his header flicked off Bogle as it found the bottom corner and the right-back was given the goal.
Leeds' number nine did not have to wait long to make sure he did score for the fifth consecutive league game at Elland Road.
Calvert-Lewin bulldozed his way past Sven Botman before sliding the ball under Lukas Hornicek in the Newcastle goal.
Anton Stach should have added a fourth early in the second period when he pounced on a slack Hornicek pass out from the pack but dinked the ball just wide.
Okafor did make it 4-0 before the hour mark when he volleyed in from the edge of the box after Newcastle failed to clear a long throw.
"Perfect start right now with eight points, terrific performance," said Leeds boss Daniel Farke. "Energy, quality and good structure in and without possession."
Bazoumana Toure netted a consolation in stoppage time to reduce Newcastle's arrears, but the damage was long since done.
Victory takes Farke's men behind only defending champions Arsenal and Manchester City.
Newcastle remain on five points but slip down to 12th due to their negative goal difference.

item.title: In-form Malen fires Roma to Serie A summit, Inter on their heels
item.description:
Netherlands striker Donyell Malen scored his sixth goal of the season as Roma moved to the top of the Serie A table with a 2-0 win over Torino on Monday, as Inter beat Udinese 5-3 to keep up with the pace in the race for the Scudetto.
Ex-Aston Villa forward Malen netted just before half-time to maintain his side's perfect start to the campaign, with four victories from as many outings.
Italy midfielder Niccolo Pisilli doubled his account for the campaign to make sure of all three points in the 93rd minute.
Torino are in 14th spot in the standings having won just once this season, beating Fiorentina last time out.
In Milan, France attacker Marcus Thuram scored and provided an assist in Inter's victory over Udinese but sit in second on goal difference behind Gian Piero Gasperini's side, before they meet next weekend.
Inter trailed 2-0 after just 16 minutes at the San Siro following efforts from Ireland defender James Abankwah and Dutch midfielder Jurgen Ekkelenkamp.
By half-time they were all-square thanks to firstly Carlos Augusto and then Nicolo Barella, from a Thuram pass.
Thuram was on the scoresheet just before the hour mark before young Italy striker Pio Esposito and Ivory Coast attacker Ange-Yoan Bonny in the final 23 minutes maintained their good start to the campaign.
Senegalese forward Idrissa Gueye claimed a late consolation for the visitors in injury time.
One stand-out negative for Inter was England centre-back John Stones leaving the field early injured, with the trip to the capital city coming up on Saturday.
Elsewhere, Cesc Fabregas' Como are third after overcoming Parma 2-1 thanks to efforts from Spanish centre-back Jacobo Ramon and Brazilian left-back Kaiki.
On Sunday, Napoli's losing run came to an end as Slovakia midfielder Stanislav Lobotka scored to earn a 1-0 win over Bologna to ease pressure on coach Massimiliano Allegri.
Sassuolo's Montenegro midfielder Vasilije Adzic scored a last-gasp winner against his parent club to consign Juventus to their first defeat of the season after a 3-2 thriller.

Asif Nazrul says World Cup withdrawal was mainly his decision
item.description:
Bangladesh boycotted the T20 World Cup held in India and Sri Lanka in February-March this year. The decision not to travel to the World Cup was mainly taken by Professor Asif Nazrul, the then adviser for youth and sports in the interim government. He has also said this publicly several times in the past.

After an investigation committee’s report on the incident was published, Asif Nazrul once again took responsibility for the decision in a Facebook post. At the same time, the former adviser questioned the investigation into the entire incident and the decision to publish its findings.

After the current government came to power, Youth and Sports Minister Aminul Haque formed a three-member investigation committee to find out why Bangladesh did not travel to play in the World Cup.

The committee’s report was presented at a press conference at the National Sports Council today, Tuesday by its head, AKM Wali Ullah, additional secretary of the Ministry of Youth and Sports. The other two members were former Bangladesh cricket captain and current BCB chief selector Habibul Bashar and Supreme Court lawyer Barrister Faisal Dastgir.

The 22-page report did not explicitly state who was responsible for Bangladesh’s decision to boycott the World Cup. However, when journalists asked at the press conference whose decision in the government had led to Bangladesh not playing in the World Cup, they were told that the decision had been taken by Professor Asif Nazrul.

Bangladesh’s absence in World Cup raises concerns over cricket's future: WCA

Page 19 of the report states that such a decision should not be taken by a single individual. Although the report does not clarify who this ‘single individual’ was, Barrister Faisal Dastgir said at the press conference that they were referring to the then sports adviser Asif Nazrul. Asked who bore the main responsibility for the decision not to play in the World Cup, Wali Ullah said, “It was the government’s decision. What else can I say!”

A few hours after the investigation report was published, former sports adviser Professor Asif Nazrul clarified his position in a Facebook post.

In his Facebook post, he wrote, “As the sports minister at the time, the decision not to travel to India to play in the T20 World Cup was mainly mine. I have said this publicly several times myself. So I do not understand why, after all this time, the Ministry of Sports felt the need to conduct such a high-profile investigation into the matter and publish it.”

Background to the decision

Explaining the background to the decision, Asif Nazrul wrote, “The incident began with Mustafiz being humiliatingly dropped from the IPL on the instructions of the Indian cricket board under pressure from Hindu extremists. Immediately afterwards, we expressed our reluctance to travel to India for the World Cup, citing concerns over security and protesting the humiliation of Bangladesh.”

Citing an ICC report to support his concerns, he further wrote, “The ICC’s first report itself acknowledged that our concerns were not unfounded. It mentioned three reasons for security concerns in India: if Mustafiz was in the World Cup squad, if Bangladeshi supporters were allowed to move around freely, and given the situation in Bangladesh ahead of the election. BBC Bangla also published an exact Bengali translation of that report. Given this situation, why would we go to India to play?”

Referring to efforts to play the World Cup at another venue, the former adviser said, “We made many attempts to play the World Cup at another venue. We also received support from some countries. But perhaps because of Indian dominance under the leadership of the ICC, it ultimately did not happen. Most importantly, there was no communication from the Indian authorities about bringing us to India to play.”

Explaining the reasoning behind the decision, he wrote, “There were three things that were absolutely clear behind my decision: the dignity of the country, the safety of our cricketers, journalists and supporters, and maintaining stability in the country’s situation ahead of the next election. At the time, it was said that if we did not play in the World Cup, Bangladesh’s matches against foreign teams would be stopped. Various initiatives by our cricket board eventually dispelled that concern as well.”

Claiming that the decision he took was the right one, Asif Nazrul said, “I believe we made the right decision. It is not right to expect that because we are a small country, someone can humiliate us as they please and we will always accept it silently. I believe in friendship with India on the basis of equal dignity, not in bowing our heads and accepting everything.”

item.title: No Mirza Shamaruh, Mirza Faisal collects nomination form
item.description:
Three people, including Mirza Faisal Amin, younger brother of President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, have collected Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) nomination forms to contest as the party’s candidate in the by-election for the Thakurgaon-1 constituency. The other two are Obaidullah Masud and Sultanul Ferdous Chowdhury (Nomro).

The interested candidates collected their nomination forms from the BNP central office in Naya Paltan, Dhaka, on Tuesday. They must complete and submit the forms on Wednesday, 16 September. The final candidate will then be announced at a meeting of the BNP’s National Standing Committee (Nomination Board) on the evening of 18 September.

The seat became vacant after former BNP secretary general and current President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir became president. The Election Commission has announced that the by-election will be held on 29 October.

Mirza Fakhrul elected 23rd president of Bangladesh

Of the three people who collected nomination forms, Mirza Faisal Amin is currently president of Thakurgaon district BNP. He previously served as mayor of Thakurgaon municipality. Obaidullah Masud and Sultanul Ferdous Chowdhury are both vice-presidents of the district BNP.

Obaidullah Masud is a former Chhatra Dal leader and also served as vice-president and general secretary of the Thakurgaon Government College students’ union. Sultanul Ferdous previously served as chairman of Thakurgaon Sadar upazila parishad. He was also once general secretary of Thakurgaon district Jatiya Party.

Since Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir became president, there had been speculation over who would succeed him in the Thakurgaon-1 constituency.

Alongside his younger brother Mirza Faisal Amin, the name of Mirza Shamaruh, Mirza Fakhrul Islam’s elder daughter, had also been discussed locally. However, the Mirza family had made no statement on the matter. Mirza Shamaruh did not collect a party nomination form.

item.title: July families hail verdict, seek swift execution
item.description:
Families of those killed in the July-August 2024 uprising and movement figures yesterday welcomed the death sentences against Obaidul Quader and six other Awami League leaders, but said justice would remain incomplete until the fugitives were brought back and the verdict implemented.
Relatives of the victims described the International Crimes Tribunal-2 ruling as a long-awaited step towards justice, while witnesses and former movement coordinators called for immediate efforts to arrest the convicts and carry out their sentences.
The reactions came after the tribunal sentenced all seven fugitive leaders to death for crimes against humanity committed during the July-August 2024 mass uprising.
Mosharraf Hossain, father of July uprising victim Meherunnesa Tanha, who was present at the tribunal when the judgment was delivered, said he was satisfied but wanted the convicts arrested and the sentences carried out.
He also welcomed the order confiscating half the assets of five convicts for compensation to July victims and their families, urging that the money be distributed through the July Foundation.
Mahin Sarkar, a former coordinator of the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement and a witness in the case, described the judgment as “historic”, but said its significance would depend on implementation.
He called on the government to bring the fugitives back to Bangladesh and execute the sentences without delay.
Political analyst and prosecution witness Ashraf Kaiser said the verdict would bring peace to those killed, injured or permanently disabled in the uprising.
Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam also expressed satisfaction, saying the majority of the four charges against each accused had been proved beyond reasonable doubt.
State-appointed defence lawyers also voiced dissatisfaction.
Israt Jahan, who represented four of the convicts, said she respected and accepted the tribunal’s decision but was “not satisfied” with it.
M Hasan Imam, who represented Quader, AFM Bahauddin Nasim and Mohammad Ali Arafat, similarly said the defence had presented its arguments on issues including command responsibility but he could not be satisfied with the outcome.
The fallout also reached Bangladesh’s relations with India.
Prime Minister’s Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman said the handover of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, Quader and others sought by Bangladesh was a crucial condition for easing relations with New Delhi.
“We are seeking Sheikh Hasina; why wouldn’t we seek Obaidul Quader and the others as well?” he said, calling on India to consider the issue “for the sake of a working engagement with Bangladesh”.

item.title: Man hacked to death while getting haircut in Keraniganj
item.description:
A 24-year-old man was hacked to death while getting a haircut at a salon in Arshinagar, Keraniganj, Dhaka, around 3pm on Tuesday.
The deceased, Farhad Hossain, was the son of Md Babul Hossain of Dularhat Police Station in Bhola. He sold fish in the Mohammadpur area and lived in Membergoli, Arshinagar.
Akhtar Hossain, who took Farhad to hospital, said he was Farhad’s cousin and that they used to move around together.
Akhtar said Farhad and 2 others went to a salon around noon. While Farhad was getting a haircut, the other 2 left to attend to another matter.
Shortly afterward, Akhtar went to the front of the salon and found Farhad lying on the road covered in blood. He took Farhad to Bangladesh Medical College Hospital, from where he was transferred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.
Akhtar alleged that several people, including local residents Sabbir, Sohel, Arman, Kallu, Rana and Ramiz, attacked Farhad with sharp weapons and shot him before leaving him on the road.
He said they had a longstanding dispute with Farhad and had demanded extortion money from him several times.
Md Habibur Rahman, inspector-in-charge of the Dhaka Medical College Hospital Police Outpost, confirmed the death and said the body had been kept in the morgue for an autopsy.
Meanwhile, a local source claimed that the killing was allegedly orchestrated by Arif alias “Chapa Arif,” described as a leading heroin dealer in Mohammadpur.
According to the source, Arif operates a large drug-selling spot in Cancer Goli in Rayerbazar.
The source said Farhad and his associates had prevented drug sales at the spot over the past few days while demanding extortion money. The spot was subsequently kept closed, and the source claimed the killing may have resulted from the dispute.

item.title: Probe report: Asif Nazrul made sole decision to skip T20 World Cup
item.description:
Bangladesh’s decision to skip the last T20 World Cup in India was taken solely by the former Youth and Sports Adviser Asif Nazrul, according to a probe committee report.
The report, prepared by a committee formed by the National Sports Council, was released on Tuesday.
It said neither the government’s highest level nor the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) board of directors had taken any decision to withdraw the national team over security concerns in India.
According to the 22-page report, Asif Nazrul, who was then in charge of the Sports Ministry, unilaterally instructed the team not to travel to India, citing security risks, without any independent assessment.
The committee interviewed 12 people, including T20 captain Litton Kumar Das, Test captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, former captain and current BCB President Tamim Iqbal Khan, former BCB general secretary and former Asian Cricket Council secretary general Syed Ashraful Haque, BCB Chief Executive Nizam Uddin Chowdhury, coach Mohammad Salahuddin and then BCB director and head of cricket operations Nazmul Abedin Fahim.
It also interviewed Youth and Sports Secretary Md Mahbub-ul-Alam and four sports journalists’ representatives.
The committee said it tried to contact Asif Nazrul and then BCB President Aminul Islam Bulbul, but received no response.
Speaking at a press conference, probe committee member and Supreme Court lawyer Barrister Faisal Dastgir said Mustafizur Rahman’s exclusion from the IPL was a decision concerning India’s domestic league and should not be linked to an international tournament.
He said Asif Nazrul simply conveyed his decision at a meeting with the cricketers.
“The person behind the decision was Professor Dr Asif Nazrul,” Dastgir said, adding, “Bangladesh should definitely have participated in the World Cup.”
The report said such an important decision should not be taken by a single individual.
“Such a decision should be made after detailed discussions with all relevant authorities, keeping in mind the future of the cricketers and the expectations of millions of cricket fans across the country,” it said.
Ahead of the national election, Asif Nazrul attended a ceremony on February 10 marking the Bangladesh Cricket Board’s (BCB) Tk2 crore donation for the development of Dhaka University’s Central Physical Education Centre ground. At the event, he said the decision not to participate in the World Cup had been taken by the BCB and the cricketers.
“There is no room for regret or questions. The decision was taken by Bangladesh’s players and the cricket board. They made sacrifices for the sake of the country’s cricket, the safety of the cricketers and Bangladesh’s dignity. It will set an example for others,” he said.
However, on January 22, Asif Nazrul had said the government had decided not to send the cricketers to India due to security concerns.
According to the report, he changed his position just three weeks later and shifted responsibility for the decision to the board and the players.
The probe committee said the incident highlighted several important lessons for Bangladesh’s cricket administration, including the need for a clearer administrative framework, effective diplomatic communication, better coordination among stakeholders and long-term planning in making such decisions.
The three-member committee comprised Youth and Sports Ministry Additional Secretary (Administration Wing) Dr AKM Oli Ullah, Supreme Court lawyer Barrister Faisal Dastgir, and former national captain and current chief national selector Habibul Bashar.

item.title: State minister Humaiun Kobir visits actress Badhon
item.description:
Actress Azmeri Haque Badhon has returned home after being attacked in Italy. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir visited her residence to inquire about her wellbeing. Badhon disclosed the matter in a Facebook post on Tuesday evening, saying the state minister visited her home on behalf of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
“Today, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir visited our home on behalf of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to inquire about me and my family. I am deeply honoured and grateful for his sincerity, courtesy and sense of responsibility,” she wrote.
She said the state’s initiative to stand by her family during the difficult time had reassured her personally and strengthened her trust in the state as a citizen.
“Security, dignity and rights of a citizen should never be compromised, regardless of differences in opinion,” she said.
Badhon also expressed gratitude to the Bangladesh government, the prime minister, the Bangladesh Embassy, the Italian government and police, and everyone at home and abroad who checked on her and her family and extended humanitarian assistance and support.
She said the experience had reminded her that “unity, courage and a sense of responsibility towards one another” are the greatest strengths against injustice, fear and division.
“When people unite for justice and truth, their strength to stand against injustice increases manifold,” she said.
Badhon also said building a safe, dignified, democratic and humane Bangladesh is a collective responsibility.

item.title: Zubaida Rahman visits Blue Sky School for children with special needs
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s wife and Ziaur Rahman Foundation Vice Chairman Dr Zubaida Rahman visited Blue Sky School, a specialized school for children operated by the Bangladesh Air Force in Dhaka Cantonment, on Tuesday.

During the visit, Zubaida Rahman observed various class activities and was briefed on therapy programs for children with special needs.
She visited the school’s hydrotherapy, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, psychology and music therapy activities.
A total of 28 specially trained teachers and therapists conduct these activities at Blue Sky School to help children with special needs lead healthy and normal lives.

Blue Sky School was established in 2021 at the initiative of the Bangladesh Air Force Women Welfare Association (BAFWWA). Classes are currently conducted with 1 teacher and 1 sister/brother for a maximum of 5 students.
Since 2021, many students with special needs have been integrated into mainstream education. Some children have also been employed as assistant therapists under the technical education program to help them become economically self-reliant.
Later, Zubaida Rahman visited BAFWWA Corner, which features various activities of BAFWWA. She was briefed on the training activities of BAFWWA Crafts and Boutique, BAFWWA Long-term Training Project and BAFWWA Industrial Home, and observed various handicraft products made by trainees.
After the visit, Zubaida Rahman attended a cultural program organized with the participation of children with special needs from Blue Sky School and students of BAFWWA Golden Eagle Nursery.
Zubaida Rahman praised the facilities provided for children with special needs at Blue Sky School and the initiatives taken by BAFWWA to develop women’s skills and support their economic self-reliance.

item.title: MJF voices concern over rising rape, abuse of women, children
item.description:
Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) has condemned the repeated incidents of rape, abuse and killing of women and children across the country.
The human rights organisation also expressed deep shock and outrage over the reported rape and killing of a seven-year-old child in Jamalpur’s Madarganj.
According to police, the child was sexually assaulted and killed, and her body was later recovered from beneath the floor of a house.
MJF also condemned this violence and expressed sympathy to the child’s family.
The Jamalpur case cannot be treated as an isolated crime, MJF said.
Recent reports of rape, sexual abuse, harassment and killing of women and children across Bangladesh point to an alarming pattern. The same questions remain: are children and women safe in homes, schools, educational institutions and communities, and are those responsible brought to justice without delay?
Recent data reinforce the seriousness of the situation. In August 2026, the Human Rights Support Society recorded violence against at least 249 women and children, including 79 rape victims, 46 of whom were children.
Ain o Salish Kendra also reported that at least 400 women were raped between January and July 2026, with 37 killed after rape. These figures represent reported cases and may not reflect the full extent of the violence.
Behind every statistic is a person whose safety, dignity, and rights have been violated. When such incidents disappear from public attention within days, there is a danger that extraordinary brutality begins to appear ordinary.
Violence against women and children must never be normalised.
Shaheen Anam, Executive Director of Manusher Jonno Foundation, said the repeated rape, abuse and killing of women and children is deeply alarming and unacceptable.
She said a child should be safe at home, on the way to school, in an educational institution and within the community.
"We cannot allow these incidents to become headlines for a few days and then disappear from public attention. Every case must be investigated promptly, those responsible must be held accountable, and stronger protection and prevention systems must be put in place. Parents and guardians must also remain attentive to children’s safety, listen to them carefully, and respond quickly to signs of fear, distress or risk. Protecting children requires shared responsibility from families, institutions, communities and the State,” Anam added.
MJF has consistently maintained that protection cannot depend only on action after a crime has occurred.
It has called for violence against women and children to be treated with the urgency of a national emergency and for stronger preventive measures, including functioning Sexual Harassment Committees in madrasas and other educational institutions.
MJF calls on the relevant authorities to ensure prompt and impartial investigation, fair and timely prosecution, and accountability in every case. Survivors and affected families must have access to medical care, psychosocial support, legal assistance, and protection, with their privacy and dignity respected.
Institutions responsible for children must maintain effective safeguarding and safe complaint mechanisms.
The Jamalpur case must not become another tragedy that fades from public attention. MJF calls for sustained action by the State, institutions and society to protect the rights, dignity and safety of women and children.

‘An Apple Tree Inside the Head’: A film exhibition with no film in it
item.description:
Alliance Française de Dhaka is showing photographs from 'An Apple Tree Inside the Head,' the unreleased feature by director Fazly Rabbi Mridha.
The film itself has no release date. What's on view instead are stills taken during its production. Images are meant to stand in for a story a visitor will never actually watch.
The exhibition is presented by Goopy Bagha Productions Limited and Views & Vision Production.
It opened on 15 September. The opening drew anthropologist Dr Manosh Chowdhury, actor Jayita Mahalanobish, and independent filmmaker Josim Ahmed, who produced the film and founded Views & Vision.
Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
The premise is the unusual part. There's no screening, no trailer, just photographs from the shoot, chosen to suggest mood and character without giving away plot.
Producer Arifur Rahman has said the decision came out of frustration with how conventional distribution works, arguing it doesn't always get a film to its widest possible audience.
The exhibition, in his framing, lets people "walk into a room" and encounter the film on entirely different terms. It will build their own sense of it rather than being told what it is.
That's a workaround worth noting on its own terms. Bangladesh's independent film scene doesn't really have a template for this. The usual route is festivals, censor clearance, then a theatrical or streaming release, assuming one comes at all.
Showing production stills before the film exists anywhere else is a bet that a story can travel and build some appetite for itself through images alone.
The film's plot leans on the oldest story going: Adam, Eve, and the apple. Mintu Mridha is convinced his wife Jasmin and son Shohag have been possessed by something. They've taken to wandering off without explanation, moving through their days like they're somewhere else.
He goes to a saint, who gives him a blessed apple, said to heal. He doesn't eat it. It just sits there. As things keep repeating in ways he can't explain, the apple starts to read as "cure," "temptation," and "omen" all at once, and the line between what's supernatural and what's simply psychological breaks down.
Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
It's that unresolved quality the exhibition seems built to carry over.
An apple that means several things at once: a family that might be haunted or might just be unwell. The photographs aren't standing in for the plot; they're an attempt to hold that ambiguity in a single frame, the way a film would hold it across two hours.
This isn't new territory for Mridha. His previous feature, Payer Tolay Maati Nai, won the Gautam Buddha Award for Best Feature Film at the 5th Nepal International Film Festival and picked up a Special Jury Mention for Best Debut Film at the 7th Jaffna International Cinema Festival in Sri Lanka.
Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
Both films share an interest in what's happening inside a character's head rather than in front of the camera.
Three producers are credited on An Apple Tree Inside the Head: Bijon Imtiaz, Arifur Rahman, and Josim Ahmed.
The organizers describe the project as part of a push to get auteur-driven South Asian films in front of international audiences. Whether the film ever reaches a festival, a theatre, or a streaming platform is still an open question.
An Apple Tree Inside the Head runs until September 19 at La Galerie, Alliance Française de Dhaka, 26 Mirpur Road, Dhanmondi. The exhibition is open to all, daily from 3pm to 9pm.
