Mir Shahe Alam: Govt unaware of EC’s UP election date announcement
item.description:
State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam has said the government has no knowledge of the Election Commission’s plan to hold Union Parishad (UP) elections in seven phases.
He made the remarks while speaking to journalists at the Secretariat on Tuesday morning, a day after Election Commissioner Abul Fazl Md Sanauallah announced the tentative schedule for the elections. “The government knows nothing about the announcement of the UP election dates. The Local Government Ministry is also unaware of it,” the state minister said.
He said there had been no correspondence between the government and the Election Commission regarding the election schedule, nor had there been any discussion through other channels.
“The Election Commission is an independent body and has the constitutional authority to conduct elections,” Mir Shahe Alam said.
He added that, under the usual practice, the EC discusses local government elections with the government before announcing the schedule. Preparatory meetings and law and order committee meetings are also held, involving issues such as the budget.
“But no such discussion has taken place between the Election Commission and the government or the Local Government Ministry,” he said.
On Monday, Election Commissioner Abul Fazl Md Sanauallah said the UP elections would be held in seven phases, with the first phase tentatively scheduled for November 12.
Speaking to journalists at the Election Commission building in Agargaon, he said the first phase would mark the beginning of the local government elections.
The tentative dates for the subsequent phases are December 13, December 30, January 17, February 4, April 22 and May 27.
The EC had earlier planned to announce the election schedule in August and begin local government elections in October.
In June, the then local government minister told Parliament that local government elections could begin across the country in phases from September or October after the monsoon season. However, the plan did not materialise.

item.title: Century-old floating vegetable market brings relief to Bagerhat farmers
item.description:
A century-old floating vegetable market in Gajalia Union of Kachua upazila in Bagerhat has become a major trading hub for farmers, with vegetables worth around Tk20-25 lakh sold in just four hours on each market day.
The market, held every Sunday and Wednesday on the Gajalia Canal, sees seasonal transactions of nearly Tk4 crore.
Rows of boats loaded with fresh cucumbers, bottle gourds, bitter gourds, ash gourds, pumpkins, ridge gourds and yardlong beans gather on the canal from early morning. Farmers sell their produce directly to wholesalers, who come from Bagerhat and neighbouring districts.
Wholesalers from Barisal, Pirojpur, Jhalakathi, Barguna and Chandpur also visit the market by boats and trawlers to purchase vegetables in bulk.
The floating market continues to preserve a traditional form of river-based commerce that was once common across rural Bangladesh.
Local traders said farmers from surrounding villages bring their produce by boat soon after dawn. They anchor along the canal and begin trading, with the number of boats increasing as the morning progresses.
By mid-morning, rows of boats stretch across the canal, with farmers and traders conducting transactions directly from the vessels.
Farmers said selling directly to wholesalers allows them to secure better prices and sell their produce quickly, reducing the risk of spoilage.
Salam Haladar, a trader from Pirojpur, said the market offers a wide range of fresh vegetables in one place.
“We can buy vegetables directly from farmers and collect large quantities at the same time. We then take them to markets in Pirojpur and other areas,” he said.
Sultan Sheikh, a trader from Barishal, said the regular presence of farmers makes it possible to purchase large quantities within a short period.
“Trading starts early in the morning and large transactions are completed within a few hours. If communication facilities improve, the volume of business could increase significantly,” he said.
Local residents said the market has been operating on the Gajalia Canal for more than 100 years. Generations of farmers have relied on it to sell vegetables grown on their land.
Rajjak Molla, a local farmer, said he brings vegetables to the market by boat on market days.
“Wholesalers buy directly from us, so our produce is sold quickly and transportation costs are relatively low. Without this market, we would have to travel to distant markets, which would cause us much more trouble,” he said.
However, poor infrastructure remains a major challenge for the market.
The road leading to the market is in poor condition, while there are no designated facilities for boats and trawlers to anchor. Farmers and traders face additional difficulties during the monsoon.
Abdullah Al Mamun, a local resident, said the market could expand significantly if basic infrastructure were improved.
“There is no proper arrangement for anchoring boats and trawlers. The road is also in poor condition. Facilities for loading and unloading goods and better market management could increase trading several times,” he said.
Mohammad Motahar Hossain, deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension in Bagerhat, said the floating market plays an important role in the local agricultural economy.
“Farmers can quickly sell their produce to wholesalers, while consumers in different areas get fresh vegetables without much delay,” he said.
He acknowledged the market's infrastructural shortcomings and said steps would be taken to address them.
The Department of Agricultural Extension is also encouraging farmers to adopt modern cultivation technologies and working to improve vegetable marketing, he added.
With improved roads, dedicated docking facilities, better loading and unloading arrangements, and stronger market management, the century-old Gajalia floating vegetable market could develop into one of the major vegetable distribution centres in southwestern Bangladesh.

item.title: Jinnah-Ghulam Azam photos pasted outside Ducsu to trample over
item.description:
Amid the ongoing controversy over the display of a photograph of Pakistan’s founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah at the Dhaka University Central Students’ Union (Ducsu) museum, photographs of Jinnah and former Jamaat-e-Islami amir Ghulam Azam were pasted on the ground outside the DUCSU building to trample over on Tuesday.
Around 2:30pm, a group of students pasted the two photographs on the floor in front of the DUCSU building. Some students then walked over the photographs in protest.
Earlier, the newly reopened Ducsu museum, following renovation, drew widespread discussion and criticism on campus after photographs of Pakistan’s founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah and Abdul Malek, a leader of the then Pakistan Chhatra Sangha, were put on display.
Amid the controversy, Abu Tayeb Habildar, a student of the Department of Urdu at Dhaka University and a candidate for the vice-president post in the 2025 DUCSU election, entered the museum on Monday afternoon, broke the frames of Jinnah’s photographs and tore them apart.
Later that afternoon, Arko Barua, organizing secretary of the Dhaka University unit of Bangladesh Chhatra Federation, put up a photograph depicting Ghulam Azam being beaten with shoes in place of Jinnah’s photographs.
Meanwhile, the Dhaka University administration has also taken a firm stance over the display of Jinnah’s photograph.
The administration said displaying photographs of individuals whose presence or legacy conflicts with the Language Movement, the historic Liberation Struggle and the core spirit of Bangladesh’s independence is unacceptable at the university or in the Ducsu museum.
It also said administrative action would be taken against those involved in the incidents in accordance with university rules.
A three-member committee, headed by Pro-Vice-Chancellor (admin), has also been formed to look into the matter.

item.title: Zahed vows to probe journo's accreditation card cancellation
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Adviser on Information and Broadcasting Dr Zahed Ur Rahman has said he will personally look into allegations that a journalist’s accreditation card was cancelled for questioning the government.
He made the comment while responding to questions from journalists at the weekly briefing at the Press Information Department (PID) conference room on Tuesday.
A journalist, referring to a recent media report, said a journalist’s accreditation card had been cancelled without the journalist or their organisation being informed of the reason.
The journalist questioned whether the decision was taken because the journalist had questioned the government.
“I don’t think this government would take any action simply because someone asked questions,” Zahed Ur Rahman said.
“You ask me questions every day. If asking questions were the reason, all of your cards would have been cancelled by now,” he added.
The adviser said the report had come to his attention and that he would investigate the matter.
“I will certainly find out why the card was cancelled and what happened. I will personally look into the matter as well,” he said.
He also claimed that the government has remained tolerant of criticism and questions, saying journalists’ right to question the government had not been restricted despite misinformation being spread about senior government officials.

item.title: Zahed: EC must coordinate with govt on local election schedule
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) will have to coordinate with the government when setting the schedule for local government elections, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Information and Broadcasting Dr Zahed Ur Rahman has said.
He also said the timeline announced by the EC should not be considered the government’s final decision.
The adviser made the comments while answering questions from journalists at the Press Information Department's weekly briefing on Tuesday.
“The Constitution gives the EC the responsibility of conducting presidential and parliamentary elections. Other elections are governed by law. So, for local government elections, the EC will have to proceed in coordination with the government,” he said.
Asked about differences between the government and the EC over the local election schedule, Jahed said there was no reason to view the issue as a conflict.
“The government’s decision is important in this election. The parliamentary election is different, as the EC has its own constitutional mandate there,” he said.
Asked whether the EC had violated the law by announcing a timeline without consulting the government, he said: “I would not say the Election Commission has violated the law. You can ask the EC for an explanation on the matter.”
The government has not yet made a final decision on the election date, he said, adding that preparations and the overall situation would be considered before setting the schedule.
“The elections will definitely be held. There is no confusion about that,” he said.
The adviser also said the upcoming local government elections would not be held under party symbols.
“Different political parties will support candidates, and some have already started announcing potential candidates. So there should be no confusion that the election will be competitive,” he said.
He expressed hope that the absence of party symbols would help restore competition in local elections.

item.title: Photo exhibition on CHT communities held in Dhaka
item.description:
A photo exhibition featuring the everyday lives, struggles, livelihoods and aspirations of communities in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) was held at the National Art Gallery of Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka on Tuesday.
Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) organized the exhibition, titled “Rising Hills, Beyond the Frame: A Photo Voice,” featuring more than 65 photographs produced through its Partnership for Resilient Livelihoods in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (PRLC) project.
The European Union-funded project is being implemented by MJF through 9 local partner organizations across Rangamati, Khagrachhari and Bandarban.
European Union Ambassador and Head of Delegation to Bangladesh Michael Miller said the photographs showed what project documents often cannot capture.
He said the images reflected people gaining greater choices, women and men developing sustainable sources of income, families strengthening their wellbeing, and communities becoming more aware of their rights.
He also said: “The European Union views development cooperation as a way to create conditions in which people can improve their own lives and shape their own futures through stronger capacities, better opportunities and local institutions that respond to people’s needs.”
Dr Mohammad Zakaria, director general of the NGO Affairs Bureau, said the PRLC project goes beyond conventional poverty reduction by helping vulnerable families develop sustainable and climate-smart livelihoods.
He also highlighted the role of women in the process, particularly through expanded economic opportunities and greater participation in decision-making.
UNDP Resident Representative Stephen Rodrigues said photographs provided a deeply human way of connecting people with the lives and experiences of others.
He said the exhibition effectively portrayed the lives, culture, aspirations and hopes of communities in the CHT.
Speaking on behalf of the Nagorikata Civic Engagement Fund, Katharina König said photography could be an important medium for storytelling, civic engagement and representation, particularly for marginalized communities.
UN Women Country Representative Geetanjali Singh congratulated MJF, the European Union and UNDP on the initiative and said it offered important lessons on livelihoods and integrated development. She also appreciated the exhibition’s focus on young women and leadership.
MJF Executive Director Shaheen Anam said the PRLC project aims to help 20,000 households move out of extreme poverty by improving health, nutrition and livelihoods.
She said MJF’s rights-based approach extends beyond economic support to protecting rights and ensuring access to justice when violations occur.
Shaheen Anam also urged the government to prioritize implementation of the unimplemented provisions of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord, saying this would help local communities rebuild trust and contribute more fully to the region and the country.
MJF governing board member Nirupa Dewan delivered the vote of thanks at the event.
Alongside the exhibition, 2 case-story publications and a photo catalogue were also unveiled.
The exhibition will remain open to visitors until 5pm on September 16 at the National Art Gallery.

item.title: Euromoney names HSBC ‘Best Cash Management Bank 2026 in Bangladesh’
item.description:
The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited (HSBC) Bangladesh has been voted ‘#1 Cash Management Bank in Bangladesh’ for the 17 th time with the bank securing the #1 position across all three subcategories - Products, Technology and Client Service.
HSBC has also been recognized as the #1 Cash Management Bank globally and in Asia in the Euromoney Cash Management Survey 2026, the world’s largest treasury survey, based on more than 7,500 client votes.
The recognition reflects HSBC’s continued focus on delivering high-quality cash management solutions, combining global connectivity, technology and client service to help businesses manage their payments, collections, liquidity and working capital more effectively.
HSBC improved its position across every region in this year’s survey and was ranked #1 in Asia, reinforcing its position as a leading cash management provider for businesses operating across markets.
The recognition is a proud moment for HSBC Bangladesh and reflects the confidence clients place in the bank’s ability to support their evolving treasury and cash management needs.
Through technology-enabled solutions and a connected global network, HSBC helps clients achieve more seamless collections and payments, greater visibility over their cash and stronger liquidity management across markets.
Commenting on the country wins, Md Mahbub ur Rahman, chief executive officer, HSBC Bangladesh, said: “Earning the top spot in Cash Management for 17 straight years is a proud milestone, but the real honor is the enduring trust our customers place in us. Winning across products, technology, and client service drives us to keep raising the standards for our business every day.”
Newaz Musharraf, head of global payments services, HSBC Bangladesh, said: “Winning Bangladesh’s Best Cash Management Bank is meaningful — and it recognizes how we are empowering our clients in Bangladesh through smoother collections and payments, clearer cash visibility and stronger controls as they manage local operations and cross-border payments. We’ll continue investing in secure, reliable digital capabilities that help corporate treasurers run their operations with confidence, even when markets move fast and remain dynamic.”
The Euromoney Cash Management Survey is widely recognized as an important benchmark of corporate treasury sentiment, with client feedback providing insight into the quality of cash management providers across products, technology and services.

item.title: The power-point magician
item.description:
The office in Gulshan-2 smells of freshly brewed coffee and nervous ambition. It is 9:15 a.m., and already the hum of printers, the clatter of keyboards, and the soft ping of email notifications fill the air.
At the far corner of the open-plan floor, Arif sits hunched over his laptop. His desk is cluttered: half-empty tea cups, sticky notes, a cracked mobile phone charging reluctantly. He adjusts his tie—it always feels too tight, like a noose—and clicks open PowerPoint.
The blank slide glows like an empty stage. For most people, this is a headache. For Arif, it is magic.
“Arif, I need your help.”
It is Rafiq, a senior project manager, his voice urgent. His hair sticks out in damp tufts; his shirt carries sweat marks despite the office air-conditioning.
“What is it now?” Arif asks, without looking up.
“Donors’ presentation, three p.m. The deck looks like a funeral. Dead text, ugly charts. You have to fix it.”
Arif sighs theatrically. “What’s the theme this time?”
“Climate-smart agriculture in coastal Khulna.”
Arif chuckles. “Last week it was digital health. Next week it’ll be gender-friendly solar panels.”
“Just work your magic, bhai. You know you’re the only one who can pull this off.”
By noon, Arif is in his element. He sprinkles the slides with photos of green paddy fields under golden sunlight. He inserts stock images of women smiling with tablets in their hands. He animates charts so that bars rise like skyscrapers. Words slide across the screen like dancers: resilience, innovation, sustainability.
As he works, his colleagues peek over his shoulder.
“Aré wah,” one whispers, “it looks like Hollywood!”
“Brother,” another says, “how do you make farmers in Barisal look like Silicon Valley startups?”
Arif smirks. “Simple. Donors want dreams, not dirt.”
At three, the boardroom fills. The long polished table gleams under white LED lights. Donor representatives from Europe and North America shuffle papers, sip green tea.
The managing director clears his throat. “Mr Arif will present our vision.”
Arif rises, sliding and clicking. On screen, fields shimmer, charts dance, and keywords shine in bold colors. He speaks with rehearsed pauses, his voice smooth as butter.
“Global Horizons is committed to empowering communities through climate-smart technology. Imagine: every farmer with a mobile app, every household with solar resilience, and every community linked to global markets.”
The donors nod, enchanted. One whispers to another, “Brilliant. This is exactly the innovation we need.”
By the end, applause fills the room. The MD beams. “Excellent, Arif. Simply excellent.”
Later, in the smoking zone on the terrace, Arif lights a cigarette. Rafiq joins him.
“You saved us again,” Rafiq says. “Donors loved it.”
Arif exhales smoke toward the hazy Dhaka skyline. “Of course they loved it. Who cares if the farmers never touch an app? The slide was perfect.”
Rafiq hesitates. “Don’t you worry… one day someone will check?”
Arif laughs, a short, sharp sound. “No one checks. They just want to believe. And I’m the magician who makes them believe.”
Months pass. Arif’s reputation grows. He is no longer “Assistant Officer.” He is “the magician.” Whenever there’s a donor visit, he is summoned.
He buys new shirts, polished shoes, and a motorbike. His family in Mirpur boasts, “Our Arif works with foreign bosses and talks English all day.”
But at night, when he removes his tie, he stares at himself in the mirror. The face looking back seems slightly blurred, as though even he is a projection on a screen.
One evening, the MD calls him in.
“Arif, listen carefully. We have the biggest donor of all visiting next week—the Global Development Bank. Billions at stake. If we impress them, our future is secured.”
Arif nods, a thrill running through him. “Leave it to me, Sir. I’ll prepare the masterpiece.”
“Good. But remember, this is high risk. If we fail, the whole company sinks.”
For days, Arif works like a man possessed. His cubicle glows late into the night. He chooses stock photos carefully: children smiling by floodwaters, drones flying over fields, villagers with solar lamps. He invents a slogan: From Delta to Data: Building Bangladesh’s Future.
He adds music, transitions, and glowing effects. Each slide feels alive, pulsing with promise.
Colleagues whisper, “He’s lost in it. Like a sorcerer.”
The day arrives. The boardroom is transformed: white orchids on the table, polished glasses of juice, the national flag in one corner. The Global Development Bank delegates sit stiffly in suits.
The MD smiles nervously. “Mr Arif will present our vision.”
Arif stands, adjusts his tie, and clicks.
The screen floods with light. Slides bloom like fireworks. He speaks, his voice steady, words flowing like a river.
“Bangladesh is not a victim of climate change. Bangladesh is the laboratory of resilience. Look at our innovation: AI-powered shrimp farming, digital cyclone alerts, solar micro-grids…”
The room falls silent. Delegates lean forward, mesmerized. The MD’s face glows with pride.
Slide after slide dazzles, until Arif clicks the final one: a golden sunrise over rivers, the slogan shining: From Delta to Data.
Applause erupts. The lead delegate rises. “This is visionary. We are ready to fund.”
The MD shakes Arif’s hand, eyes wet with relief. “You’ve done it, magician.”
That night, Arif walks home through Gulshan’s empty streets. Streetlights blur in the mist. His body feels heavy, but his mind buzzes.
He enters his small flat, switches on the light, and opens his laptop again.
But the screen behaves strangely. Slides shuffle on their own. Images twist, charts stretch, words dance without his command.
On the screen, his own face appears—blurred, pixelated. It speaks in his voice:
“You’ve fooled them all. But what happens when the magician believes his own magic?”
Arif stares, frozen. The voice continues:
“You promised solar panels, apps, drones. Where are they? You created worlds out of nothing. Now nothing will consume you.”
The screen flickers, then goes black.
The next morning, colleagues arrive to find Arif’s chair empty. His laptop glows with a looping slide:
A world of resilience, innovation, sustainability.
But Arif is gone. Some say he fled. Others whisper he dissolved into the slides themselves, trapped forever inside PowerPoint.
At the next meeting, when a new assistant fumbles with slides, the projector glitches. For a moment, Arif’s blurred face flickers on the wall, smiling.
And a voice echoes faintly: “Donors want dreams, not dirt.”
Haroonuzzaman is a Bangladeshi translator, novelist, poet, researcher, and academic.

item.title: RCC steps up dengue prevention efforts, urges public cooperation
item.description:
Rajshahi City Corporation (RCC) has intensified its dengue prevention activities, urging residents to work alongside the city authorities to eliminate mosquito-breeding sites and keep their surroundings clean.
The call came at an exchange meeting on dengue prevention, cleanliness drives and public awareness held at the City Hall meeting room of Nagar Bhaban on Tuesday.
RCC Administrator Mahfuzur Rahman Riton attended the meeting as the chief guest, while RCC Chief Executive Officer Rezaul Karim presided over it. Deputy Registrar of Rajshahi Medical University Dr Mofakharul Islam attended as the special guest.
Specialist doctors, entomologists, health workers and other concerned officials also took part in the meeting.
Speakers said public participation is crucial to preventing dengue, alongside the measures being taken by the city corporation.
They said Aedes mosquitoes generally breed in stagnant, clear water and urged residents to regularly inspect and clean areas around their homes, including yards, rooftops, balconies and under-construction buildings.
Residents were also advised to clean their homes and surroundings at least once a week and remove potential breeding sites such as discarded containers, tubs, coconut shells and old tyres.
“We have taken various initiatives to keep city residents safe from the risk of dengue. We all have to work together. With the cooperation of city residents, we want to build a clean, safe and dengue-free Rajshahi city,” Riton said.
He said the RCC had intensified public awareness campaigns, destruction of mosquito-breeding sites, cleanliness drives and mosquito-control activities across the city.
“City residents also have to play a vital role in preventing dengue,” he added.
Dr Mofakharul Islam said everyone should contribute to raising public awareness about dengue prevention.
Professor Dr Azizul Haque Azad, head of the Department of Medicine at Rajshahi Medical College Hospital (RMCH), said a separate ward had been arranged at the hospital following an increase in dengue cases.
He said dengue is a viral disease transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes and that people can become infected through the bite of an infected mosquito during both daytime and nighttime.
Umme Habiba, district entomologist at the Civil Surgeon’s Office, and Abdul Bari, entomological technician at the Divisional Director of Health Office, presented an overview of the dengue situation at the meeting.
Selim Reza Ranju, deputy chief cleaning officer of RCC, presented the measures taken by the city corporation to prevent dengue.
